text: At the start of the conflict, the Continental Congress created the New York (later, Northern) and Canadian Departments to exercise operational command and control in the areas of active fighting. Congress organized the Middle and Southern Departments in February 1776 as the war spread southward (Map 2). Congress appointed Maj. Gen. Charles Lee to command the Southern Department, which encompassed Virginia, the Carolinas, and Georgia. Lee’s tour of duty was short, but he played an important role in defeating then Maj. Gen. Henry Clinton’s 1776 attack on Charleston. Brig. Gen. Robert Howe of North Carolina took command of the Southern Department when Congress recalled Lee northward in June

201776. Howe lacked an explicit appointment order from Congress, an oversight that allowed state political leaders to challenge Howe’s command authority over state troops. Howe struggled to defend Georgia and South Carolina from raids out of British East Florida. Ultimately, he was recalled after the loss of Savannah and much of Georgia in late 1778.Maj. Gen. Benjamin Lincoln took command of the Southern Department in early 1779. Like Howe, Lincoln experienced significant challenges with civil-military cooperation. His tenure ended with the disastrous loss of Charleston, its garrison, and most of the southern Continental Army in May 1780. Gates took command in July 1780, and soon thereafter led his army to near ruin at Camden in August 1780. Greene thus inherited a command that in two years Map 2

21had experienced nothing but defeat; the death or imprisonment of 3,100 Continentals; the loss of Georgia and much of South Carolina; and the loss of thousands of small arms and quantities of cannons, ordnance stores, and other supplies.

Greene and Cornwallis faced serious challenges during operations across the topographically diverse area of operations—bounded by the Appalachian Mountains in the west and running about 330 miles from southern Virginia to Savannah, Georgia. Camden and Cheraw were located along the East Coast’s fall line—the highest navigable point on rivers flowing from the mountains to the Atlantic Ocean—and within the Sandhills region, a strip of broad pine barrens cut with flat ridges, stretching from Georgia to North Carolina. Savannah and Charleston were in the lower coastal plain, a mix of gently sloping terrain and wide tidal rivers bordered by marshy, fertile lowlands. In between was the upper coastal plain, with its slightly to steeply sloped clay and gravel ridges covered with thick vegetation. The Battles of Cowpens, South Carolina, and Guilford Courthouse, North Carolina, took place within this geological region. Weather and climate within the Carolina subtropical region were equally diverse. Average summertime high temperatures ranged from 95°F (35°C) in the coastal plains to 75°F (24°C) in the upper parts of the Blue Ridge Mountains. Summertime heat and humidity affected both sides but caused greater hardships for northern European soldiers who were unused to the American climate. Winter daytime highs in the upper coastal plains ranged from 52°F (11°C) to 47°F (8°C), with nighttime lows around 32°F (8°C). The highest amounts of precipitation, mostly rain except in the upper mountain elevations, occurred along the coastal plains. The lower coastal plain averaged 51 to 60 inches (130 to 152 centimeters) of rain annually, and the upper coastal plain received around 46 to 50 inches (117 to 127 centimeters) per year. Heavy rainfall, especially during the peak months of March and July, hindered the cross-country movement of

22troops and supply wagons by turning roads into mud and making normally shallow creeks and rivers impassable. Diseases like smallpox and ague (malaria) significantly affected the operations of both armies. Smallpox was endemic in eighteenth-century Europe; thus, most British troops had acquired immunity to it either from inoculation or natural exposure. By contrast, the smaller, largely rural American population was vulnerable to smallpox. Continental and militia forces at Boston and Québec in 1775 were afflicted greatly by smallpox, likely brought over by British troops. Washington subsequently ordered the inoculation of Continental soldiers, which reduced the impact of the smallpox to more manageable levels. Washington also attempted to further reduce camp fevers like typhoid by imposing strict hygiene measures in Continental encampments—practices carried over by Greene’s Continental forces in the South. The pestilent climate of the American South also plagued soldiers, as epidemics of fever derailed American offensives on British East Florida in 1776 and 1778. Clinton was acutely aware of the dangers posed by low country diseases to unacclimated Europeans and timed his 1780 attack on Charleston to take place in winter, when the risks of these illnesses were lower. The protracted American defense of the city, however, frustrated Clinton’s efforts to protect his forces. Many British and German troops fell ill from malaria, and the filth that accumulated during the siege triggered a typhoid outbreak. The movement of British troops and freed Black slaves into the interior caused smallpox outbreaks that lingered in rural areas after the end of the war. Cornwallis’s army was affected greatly by malaria, despite his efforts to avoid the disease by marching his army into the supposedly healthier up-country region. Many soldiers were permanently incapacitated, and several died from fevers. Malaria was no respecter of people, and during October 1780 both Cornwallis and Tarleton temporarily were incapacitated by ague. The northern Continental troops were equally susceptible to malaria, but their surgeons usually carried cinchona bark (also known as Jesuit’s bark) supplied from Spanish-held New Orleans. Cinchona bark contains quinine, a substance known to suppress malarial symptoms. British
23surgeons were aware of the bark’s medicinal properties but seldom received enough to make a difference.

Georgia was the youngest of the thirteen colonies, with a prewar White population of 25,000 and an enslaved Black population of similar size. Georgia’s coastal elites were overwhelmingly Anglicans—members of the established Church of England—yet the colony tolerated the presence of Jewish, Catholic, and non-Anglican Protestant settlers. After seizing power, the Georgia revolutionaries found themselves hemmed in by the Creek and Cherokee nations to the west and British-held St. Augustine in East Florida. A small radical, independence-minded bloc and a larger moderate Anglican faction reluctant to sever ties with Great Britain dominated the Georgia Whigs. During the early years of the war, Georgia patriots failed to take St. Augustine but did succeed in halting similar loyalist incursions. The patriots were aided by influential trader and Indian commissioner George Galpin, who persuaded the Lower Creek nation not to side with the British and to remain neutral during the war. Compared to Georgia, North Carolina’s prewar society was more divided politically and had fewer radical revolutionaries, owing to Royal Governor Josiah Martin’s efforts to maintain good relations with the prewar colonial elites. In addition, the Regulator movement of 1766–1771—a short-lived rebellion of backcountry Carolinians against the royal government—fostered rural resentment against the Whig-dominated state assembly. Many backcountry inhabitants were recent German and Scotch-Irish immigrants who were not interested in Whig or Tory political arguments. Lastly, the state had a significant number of Friends, also known as Quakers, and Moravians, who refused to support or serve in the militia because of their pacifist beliefs. North Carolina revolutionaries were initially few in number, but in July 1775 many North Carolinians joined their cause after Whigs circulated a report claiming that Martin would organize militia units from White loyalists and Black recruits who

had been emancipated from rebel owners. The incensed patriots drove Martin into exile aboard a British warship on the Cape Fear River. Martin responded by convincing London to dispatch reinforcements to help the loyalist militia regain North Carolina. General Clinton’s expedition reached North Carolina in March 1776, only to find the patriots had crushed a loyalist force at Moore’s Creek Bridge on 27 February 1776. The British withdrew, leaving the patriot militia free to consolidate control over North Carolina—efforts that were complicated by British-instigated Cherokee attacks on settlements along the Catawba River. In September 1776, Brig. Gen. Griffith Rutherford of North Carolina led 2,500 militiamen on a punitive expedition that, in concert with similar Virginia and South Carolina expeditions, destroyed more than thirty Cherokee settlements. Most of the displaced Cherokee fled westward and took no further part in the war.Charleston, the capital of colonial South Carolina, was established in 1670 by White settlers from Bermuda and Barbados. Although the Church of England was the official church of South Carolina, colonial proprietors shrewdly enticed French Huguenots, English and Scotch-Irish Protestants, and Sephardic Jews fleeing persecution in Europe to settle there. Prewar South Carolinian society might have been religiously diverse, but it was stratified economically between a large group of lower-class Whites and a small planter class, the so-called Rice Kings. Wealth derived from exporting rice, indigo, and other commodities gave the Rice Kings disproportionate political power and turned Charleston into the most affluent city in the colonial-era United States. By 1775, South Carolina had an estimated 170,000 inhabitants, split between 60,000 and 70,000 White people and 100,000 enslaved Black people. The upper strata of the mercantile community was overwhelmingly Anglican, yet sympathetic to Whig politics. The middle- and backcountry population of South Carolina was a diverse, boisterous mix of Protestant Scotch-Irish, and lesser numbers of Germans, Swiss, and Quakers—many who had migrated south from Virginia via the Great Wagon Road. Newer Scotch-Irish immigrants tended to remain loyal to the Crown, whereas older Scots—who

often harbored bitter memories of British brutality after the 1666 Covenanter uprising and 1745 Jacobite Rebellion—generally were hostile toward the British government and colonial establishment. Backcountry attitudes toward the British government were shaped further by the Anglo-Cherokee War of 1759. British regulars and Carolina militia troops won territorial concessions from the defeated Cherokee, but lingering resentments within rural communities gave rise to a Regulator movement that—unlike in North Carolina—extracted concessions from the colonial government peacefully. After South Carolina declared its independence, South Carolina Continental and militia units defeated a British amphibious assault against Charleston in June 1776, and other militia forces squelched Cherokee and loyalist raids in the backcountry. Consequently, South Carolina remained quiet until the British attack on Savannah in late 1778. The English colony of Virginia was established in 1607 with a settlement at Jamestown. The early colonists struggled for several years with disease, starvation, and skirmishes with the Algonquin-speaking native population. The colony began to thrive in the mid-1630s with the intense cultivation of tobacco—first by indentured Whites who gradually were supplanted by enslaved Africans. By 1775, Virginia was the most populous state in America, with about 538,000 residents, of whom 318,000 were White and 220,582 were (mostly enslaved) Black. Tobacco wealth and the organization of an elected legislature, later known as the House of Burgesses, gave the planter elites great influence over the politics and the policies of the Crown-appointed governor. Nevertheless, the colony’s overreliance on a single cash crop left the planters vulnerable to price drops, and their lavish lifestyles left them indebted to British merchants. Virginia’s rural backcountry served as the first stop for many Scotch-Irish, largely Presbyterian, moving south from the increasingly crowded eastern portions of Pennsylvania and New York. The Scotch-Irish were soon joined by bands of German Lutherans and Moravians, former New England Puritans and—after the Great Awakening of 1740—congregations of Methodists and Baptists. By contrast, the Anglican Church of England was the

colony’s official church and dominated the tidewater planters. Rising tensions over religious taxes and land grant fees were exacerbated by royal attempts to bypass the House of Burgesses and levy debt-reducing fees and taxes. Royal Governor John Murray, 4th Earl of Dunmore, dissolved the House in May 1775 but fled for his safety after patriots convened their own legislature and seized control. From the security of a British ship at Yorktown, Dunmore proclaimed martial law, offered freedom to enslaved Black people and White indentured servants who would join the loyalist cause, and organized emancipated Black volunteers into Lord Dunmore’s Ethiopian Regiment—provocative moves that alienated many otherwise sympathetic Americans. Patriot militia forces crushed Dunmore’s expedition at Great Bridge on 9 December 1775. The demoralized British soon withdrew, leaving Virginia firmly in patriot hands.Whig-controlled Virginia was left somewhat undisturbed for the next several years while the British set their focus elsewhere—which was fortunate for the Americans, as the state was vulnerable to invasion via the Chesapeake Bay’s river network. The state also lacked manpower to defend itself, as most of its Continental regiments had surrendered at Charleston in May 1780. In the meantime, Virginia played an integral part in sustaining the American war effort in the South. Smuggled Virginia tobacco helped to fund the American war effort, and Virginia farms and towns supplied provisions and militia support to the Continental Army.East Florida was not part of the original thirteen colonies but was instead ceded to Britain at the end of the Seven Years’ War. Florida’s population in 1775 was only a few thousand White people, both free and indentured, and a thousand or so enslaved Black people. Florida’s value lay in its strategic position close to Britain’s Caribbean holdings and American-held Savannah and Charleston. Both the British and Americans were surprised at the pro-loyalist sentiments among Florida’s settlers, which were strengthened by the inflow of loyalist refugees from Georgia and the Carolinas.

Greene’s assessment of the South’s infrastructure revealed that the region had few improved roads and even fewer bridges. Thus, controlling access to river fords and ferry sites was critical to unhindered movement of troops and supply columns. Greene therefore ordered Quartermaster Carrington to build a flotilla of bateaux (flat-bottomed boats) and carriages to improve operational mobility and efficiency of moving troops and supplies via inland waterways. The assessment also revealed the placements of friendly and hostile districts, as well as the location of grist mills—information necessary for collecting and processing provisions and setting up magazines for storing supplies. Greene next appointed Major Davie, a respected North Carolina militia officer, as the commissary general, the officer responsible for procuring forage and provisions from local sources. Both sides survived by requisitioning supplies from the locals, but Greene tried to mollify the locals by requiring Davie’s quartermasters to supervise foragers, prevent looting, and issue receipts for requisitioned supplies—thereby tying the holder financially to the success of the Whig cause.

text: Greene next turned to improving the state of his army of roughly 1,000 troops. The consolidated remnants of the veteran 1st and 2d Maryland Brigades under Col. Otho Holland Williams—about 400 Continentals, which formed the core of his army—were redesignated as the Maryland Brigade on 1 January 1781. Greene’s light troops consisted of a company each of Delaware and Maryland light infantry, and Col. William Washington’s amalgamated 1st and 3d Continental Light Dragoons. Aside from an understrength North Carolina Continental company and a handful of supernumerary officers, the Continental Line regiments from the southern states were dead or British prisoners in Charleston. By comparison, General Gates had commanded two Continental infantry brigades of 950 soldiers, 400 light infantry, and a 100-strong artillery detachment. Greene described his new command to his former assistant,

Col. John Cox: “On my arrival to camp I found General Gates at the head of a few ragamuffins without discipline, order or government. The officers had lost all confidence and respect for the General, the loss of discipline naturally followed.” He further noted to Alexander Hamilton how the Whigs and Tories commonly brutalized prisoners and supporters of the other side. Greene responded by issuing orders to restore discipline in the Continental ranks and backed up his orders with corporal punishment and executions of notorious offenders. Greene’s next priority was solidifying support from the state authorities in his department. Despite his best efforts to recruit local populations into Continental service, Greene found few men willing to enlist and risk ruin at home. Instead, he had to depend on a mix of alarm (immediate response) and short service (generally ninety days or less) militia, as well as state line troops enlisted in state service for up to one year. After the heavy losses incurred in Charleston, states relied heavily on the cheaper and easier options to mobilize militia and state line units to support Greene’s campaigns. Greene’s most significant source of state troops and supplies came from Virginia, so when Congress assigned Maj. Gen. Friedrich Wilhelm von Steuben to the Southern Department, Green appointed Steuben to expedite recruits and supplies and help Governor Thomas Jefferson defend his state. North Carolina was hamstrung politically by a three-way power struggle between Governor Abner Nash, the state assembly, and its Board of War—a situation that greatly hampered Greene’s ability to get supplies and manpower. Matters were worse in Georgia and South Carolina, as neither state had a functioning government. Greene had grasped the importance of maintaining good relations with the civil authorities and carried on an extensive correspondence with Continental Congress President Samuel Huntington and the state governors and officials within his department. Greene’s motivation went beyond obtaining recruits and supplies; he also intended to demonstrate support for legitimate American governance. Greene quickly realized that his success depended greatly on support and cooperation from South Carolina militia officers like Thomas Sumter, Francis Marion, and Andrew Pickens. Sumter was

a Virginia native who saw service during the Cherokee War before settling along the Santee River. He grew wealthy through his country store and marriage to Mary Jameson, a well-to-do widow. After serving in the Continental Congress, Sumter commanded South Carolina Continentals until he resigned in 1778. After loyalists burned his plantation in May 1780, Sumter organized a partisan corps and was commissioned commander in chief of the South Carolina militia. During the latter part of 1780, Sumter’s partisans raided loyalist outposts and convoys and fought several engagements with Tarleton’s Legion. Known as the “Gamecock,” Sumter was a prideful, charismatic, hard-fighting—albeit strategically inept and stubborn—patriot leader who often refused to cooperate with Greene’s plans. Greene had more success with the other South Carolina partisan leaders. Andrew Pickens was a reticent Scotch-Irish Presbyterian planter from the Long Cane district of South Carolina. He raised a unit of fellow Cherokee War veterans that fought successfully against Cherokee raiders and loyalists at Kettle Creek. Pickens accepted parole after the surrender of Charleston but returned to active service after Tories burned his property. Francis Marion was a South Carolina native of French Huguenot descent and a planter on the Santee River. He saw service during the French and Indian War and the Cherokee War, which led to a captaincy in the 2d South Carolina Continentals in June 1775. Marion commanded Continental troops through major operations in 1779–1780, but he avoided the surrender of Charleston because he was outside the city recovering from a broken ankle. After the Waxhaws massacre, Marion organized a partisan band that carried out irregular warfare. Unlike Sumter, Marion proved adept at low-cost raids against loyalist units, and even against Tarleton’s best Legion dragoons.With his lieutenants busy with improvements, Greene had time to assess his strategy and campaign plans. The Continental Army’s position at Charlotte made tactical sense, as the town sat in a patriot-supporting district and blocked Cornwallis’s route to the loyalist enclaves at Salisbury and Cross Creek. However, Greene’s small army was critically short of weapons, ordnance stores, provisions, and forage. Greene needed time without major combat action to

restore the fighting potential of his Continentals and improve the army’s receipt of supplies and provisions—neither of which would be possible at Charlotte. Yet a withdrawal from Charlotte would embolden the British and loyalists and dispirit the local Whigs. Thus, Greene had to figure out a way to regroup the army while sustaining the morale of Whig supporters and undermining that of the loyalists. Greene explained his predicament to Brig. Gen. Henry Knox, Washington’s chief of artillery: Nothing can save this Country but a good permanent Army conducted with great Prudence and Caution. . . . Every thing here depends upon opinion, and it is equally dangerous to go forward as to stand still for if you lose the Confidence of the People you lose all Support and if you rush into danger you hazard every Thing. Greene addressed his dilemma by adopting what was described as “the most audacious and ingenious piece of military strategy of the war” by sending Morgan’s “flying army”—a mix of roughly 800 Continental and militia infantry, light infantry, and dragoons—west of the Broad River. Greene’s orders to Morgan, who had been promoted to brigadier general in October, were specific: “The object of this detachment is to give protection to that part of the country and spirit up the people . . . act offensively or defensively as your own prudence and direction many direct . . . annoy the enemy in the quarter [and] collect the provisions and forage out of the way of the enemy.” Greene’s orders illustrate his grasp of the importance of maintaining the goodwill of the population, without which no victory was possible. While Morgan’s men marched westward, Greene temporarily took his remaining troops to a “camp of repose” in the fertile and patriot-friendly Cheraw Hills region of South Carolina on the Pee Dee River, where he would rebuild the fighting strength and morale of his Continental infantry through strict discipline and training. Greene’s movement to Cheraw Hills included quartermaster wagons with supplies like provisions and uniforms, ordnance

wagons for ammunition and spare weapons, and hospital wagons for carrying wounded and sick soldiers and medical supplies. Greene appointed quartermaster and ordnance officers to supervise the work primarily performed by civilian specialists. Among this last group were women, which included soldiers’ wives who were carried “on the strength” of the regiments—authorized rations and permission to accompany their husbands—in exchange for handling routine sustainment tasks like washing and sewing uniforms. Commanders prioritized women capable of working as nurses and medical attendants. Brig. Gen. Nathanael Greene, Jacques Reich, c. 1899–1920 (National Portrait Gallery, Smithsonian Institution)

The British army was not idle in its winter camp at Winnsboro, South Carolina. Cornwallis and his quartermasters gathered the necessary supplies while the officers and sergeants supervised the training of those troops not down with camp sickness. Cornwallis commanded about 8,000 regulars and provincials—mostly American and Irish immigrants with some Continental deserters, all of whom generally had enlisted for the duration of the war—but had only 2,000 troops at Winnsboro. The remainder were tied down as garrisons for Ninety Six and other critical bases because Cornwallis did not trust the loyalty and efficiency of the loyalist militia levies. The numbers changed constantly as Cornwallis and his officers shifted forces to counter partisan attacks. Cornwallis’s position at Winnsboro made tactical sense, as he was well placed to reinforce Ninety Six and Camden quickly. Yet the town lay above the fall line, which forced quartermasters to move supplies by wagon convoys that made lucrative targets for Whig insurgents. Being immersed in tactical matters, Cornwallis lost sight of his strategic objective of recruiting and safeguarding loyalist levies and their families in South Carolina. Loyalist morale suffered as a result, as evidenced by significant levels of desertion and poor combat performance against patriot militia detachments. Lt. Col. Henry “Light Horse Harry” Lee’s 2d Partisan Corps and Col. Francis Marion’s partisan detachment opened the offensive with un-successful attacks on British posts in South Carolina at Georgetown and Fort Watson in January and April 1781, respectively. The attacks forced Cornwallis to react by sending reinforcements to shore up the defenses in what once had been safe rear areas. Col. William

Washington’s corps of Continental dragoons and militia light infan-try defeated a detachment of 250 loyalists at Hammond’s Store—a crossroads settlement near present-day Clinton, South Carolina—in December 1780. Meanwhile, Morgan’s flying army had openly crossed the Broad River and raised the alarm by raiding loyalist farms for provisions and forage. Morgan’s initial success led to his proposal to drive westward into Georgia. Greene tactfully rejected the proposal as too risky but added: “If moving as far as Ninety Six, or any where in the neighborhood of it, will contribute to the ob-taining of more ample supplies, you have my consent. Col. Tarleton is said to be on his way to pay you a visit. I doubt not but he will have a decent reception and a proper dismission.”Tarleton’s British Legion was indeed riding hard to corner Morgan’s elusive flying army. Cornwallis sent reinforcements along to Tarleton along with fresh orders to pass the Broad River: “with the legion and the first battalion of the 71st, as soon as possible. If Morgan is still at Williams’ or anywhere else within your reach, I should wish you to push him to the utmost. . . . Ninety Six is of so much consequence, that no time is to be lost.” Ninety Six was important strategically to the British to maintain secure communications with Cherokee allies to the west, protect loyalist allies, and suppress rebel partisans.Thus reinforced, Tarleton commanded a mixed-arm force of the 7th Foot (Royal Fusiliers—177 officers and men), 71st Foot (Fraser’s Highlanders—263 troops), a composite Light Infantry Battalion (135–180 men), the British Legion infantry battalion (200–271 soldiers), 300 dragoons, and a light artillery detachment. Additional support came from loyalist scouts and civilian wagon teamsters and drivers.Tarleton’s pursuit was delayed by bad weather, which gave his troops time to glean barely five days of provisions from that left by the American foraging parties. Scouts commanded by Col. Andrew Pickens reported Tarleton’s advance to Morgan on 12 January 1781, who responded by consolidating his scattered detachments by Thicketty Creek. In line with Greene’s instructions to avoid decisive engagement, Morgan directed his army northward to the Broad River via the Green River Road—a movement calculated to draw Tarleton away from possible reinforcements. Meanwhile, Morgan
asked Pickens to screen the withdrawal and sweep supplies away from the Legion’s march route.

Morgan’s army camped at Thicketty Creek, about 13 miles from the Broad River, on the night of 15–16 January 1781. On the same evening, under cover of darkness, Tarleton’s troops made a surprise crossing of the Pacolet River. Morgan learned early on 16 January that Tarleton’s troopers were across the Pacolet, and he quickly calculated the enemy would close the distance to the American rear guard before the flying army could cross the Broad River safely. Morgan thus opted to set up a deliberate defense at the Cowpens, a well-known cattle-grazing field off the Green River Road. En route, Morgan called up the local militia as reinforcements for the expected battle.That evening, Morgan’s troops ate and rested while the officers and sergeants supervised issuing ammunition—twenty-four rounds per militiaman and forty per Continental soldier—and weapons preparations. In the interim, Morgan rode the ground with his subordinate commanders to discuss disposition and tactics for the impending battle. Morgan then held a council of war to issue final orders and a rousing demand to crush the hated enemy. Morgan afterward “went among the volunteers, helping them fix their swords, joked with them about their sweet-hearts, told them to keep in good spirits . . . and telling them the old wagoner would crack his whip over [Tarleton] in the morning. . . . ‘Just hold up your heads, boys, three fires . . . and you are free.’”While Morgan’s troops rested, Tarleton briefly paused to let his units rest and eat what little remained of their provisions. Tarleton resumed his advance before morning twilight on 17 January, with a strong light infantry advance guard. Partisan scouts reported the British advance, and Morgan sent out a dragoon patrol, known as a vidette, to make contact and delay the enemy advance. After a brief engagement, Tarleton’s troopers captured several American skirmishers, who yielded information about Morgan’s bivouac site.

The skirmish put the loyalist and British troops on edge, and they advanced slowly for fear of further ambushes. Meanwhile, the Americans woke before dawn, ate a quick breakfast, and shook out their battle lines (Map 3). Morgan carefully arrayed his well-rested and motivated forces to maximize each other’s strengths while minimizing their vulnerabilities. Morgan first deployed 270 rifle-armed skirmishers on a forward slope facing the expected British advance along the Green River Road. Morgan next positioned the remaining 700 Carolina, Georgia, and Virginia militiamen along the reverse slope under the overall command of Pickens. Thus positioned, the American militia had better chances of hitting the enemy troops silhouetted on the higher ground, whereas the British were more likely to overshoot the Americans. Morgan then deployed his third line of Continental, North Carolina, and Virginia State troops—a provisional battalion commanded by Lt. Col. John Eager Howard of the 1st Maryland Regiment—far enough beyond the militia position to avoid detection, even by Legion dragoons on horseback. Lastly, Washington’s 3d Legionary Corps, with attached mounted militiamen, took position behind the third line, ready to counterattack any British breakthrough. To this point, no Continental commander had successfully employed southern militia troops using conventional tactics. Morgan was an experienced light infantry commander who had instead learned how to employ militia troops effectively in conventional operations. Morgan would use the militia to conduct a delaying defense, trading space for time while inflicting maximum casualties in the enemy ranks. In the first line, the skirmishers had orders to fire two shots, especially aimed at the British officers, and fall back to the main militia line. Pickens’s militia troops in the second line had the same orders to fire two shots and withdraw in good order through the loosely positioned Continental Line. At that point, Howard’s Continental and state troops in the third line would fight conventionally with their flanks covered by the regrouped militia and dragoons. By contrast, Tarleton employed little tactical finesse when he ordered a troop of Legion dragoons to “drive in the militia parties who covered the front, [so] that General Morgan’s disposition might be

conveniently and distinctly inspected.” Concentrated rifle fire from the Whig skirmishers arrested the dragoon’s advance, prompting Tarleton to position the 3-pounder “grasshopper” cannons on the Green River Road to cover the deployment of forces: the Royal Fusiliers left of the road, the Legion Infantry in the middle, and the light infantry on the right flank. A canebrake southwest of the Map 3

road forced Tarleton to position the Highlanders behind the Fusilier regiment. Tarleton anchored each flank with a troop of dragoons and held the remaining mounted troops in reserve.Tarleton ordered his infantry to advance at the quick step (100 steps per minute) to drive off the riflemen with the bayonet. The patriot skirmishers “gave them a heavy & galling Fire & retreated to the Regiments intended for their support.” Maj. Joseph McDowell, rather than joining the retreat, instead led his North Carolina skirmishers to fight from the cover of the canebrake. The Royal Artillery’s fire caused few casualties, but overshooting forced Washington to relocate his dragoons from their vulnerable position. Meanwhile, Morgan waited until the enemy line reached the killing distance of 50 yards before ordering Pickens’s militia to open fire. The effect of the close-range fire devastated the British ranks. Lt. Roderick Mackenzie, Highlander company commander, later reported: “Two-thirds of the British infantry officers had already fallen, and nearly the same proportion of privates; fatigue however, enfeebled the pursuit, much more than loss of blood.” The surviving British officers rallied their troops and resumed the advance on the American militia line.Pickens’s soldiers followed orders to break contact, with some having to run from British bayonets. Tarleton reacted to what appeared to be a routed militia line by ordering the dragoon troop on his right to pursue the fleeing rebels. The British dragoons brushed aside a screen of skirmishers and cut down several Whig militiamen before being scattered by a concentrated charge of Colonel Washington’s troopers. While Morgan rode in to rally the shaken American militiamen, the British main line advanced rapidly to engage Colonel Howard’s Continental line, now visible on the reverse slope.Tarleton reacted to the sighting of the Continental line by sending the Highlanders to extend his left flank. Meanwhile, Howard ordered sequential volleys by battalion, thereby keeping the enemy under continuous fire. The British infantry responded, and the two sides stood firm for several minutes while trading volleys. Tarleton broke the impasse by sending several Legion dragoon troops to support the

Highlanders’ movement beyond the Continental line’s right flank. Howard reacted by ordering Capt. Andrew Wallace’s flank company to “refuse the right” by pivoting 90 degrees rightward to present a wall of bayonets toward the loyalist troopers. The attacking Highlanders fired a volley just as Wallace issued his orders. In the confusion, Wallace’s company fired a volley, did an about-face, and marched to the rear. In short order, the remaining Continental units replicated the same volley and rearward movement. Howard had not intended such a movement, but he capitalized on the error to have his troops avoid the British flanking movement while reloading their weapons. Morgan was briefly alarmed by the unexpected development but was reassured when he saw the Continentals moving in good order to the rear. Morgan responded by pointing out a slight rise astride the road, where Howard was to turn about and resume the fight.While the infantry action played out in the middle, Colonel Washington regrouped his troopers after successfully driving back The Battle of Cowpens, Don Troiani, 1996, a National Guard Heritage Painting, courtesy of the National Guard Bureau

the Legion dragoons on the American right. Through the black powder smoke, Washington spotted the disordered and leaderless British infantry surging after the withdrawing Continentals. Washington recognized an opportunity to encircle the enemy and sent a courier riding to Howard with vital intelligence: “They are coming on like a mob. Give them a fire and I will charge them.” As Washington led his squadron around the exposed left flank of the Highlanders, Howard’s troops pivoted and volleyed into the faces of the shocked British troops, killing and wounding dozens and stunning the remainder. Howard’s soldiers capitalized on the confusion with a bayonet charge while Pickens’s militia and Washington’s dragoons enveloped the enemy flanks. Tarleton attempted a counterattack, but most of his dragoons—many of whom were former Continental soldiers pressed into British service after their capture—instead rode from the battlefield. Tarleton attempted a final sortie with sixty remaining dragoons, but Continental dragoons and militiamen drove him back. Tarleton rode from the battlefield to rally about 200 soldiers and returned to Cornwallis’s camp on 18 January 1781. Morgan reported the enemy losses as 10 officers and “100 rank and file killed,” 200 wounded, and 529 prisoners—almost all of Cornwallis’s best light infantry soldiers. The Americans seized valuable booty: two 3-pounder guns; 800 muskets; and 35 wagons filled with ammunition, uniforms, and other supplies. In return, the Continentals lost ten killed and fifty-five wounded, in addition to an unknown number of militia casualties.

Morgan took no time to celebrate his victory but instead prepared to move to avoid the inevitable pursuit from Cornwallis. Groups of local militiamen and prisoners buried the dead and readied the seriously wounded for transportation. With prisoners in tow, Morgan’s army left hours after the battle and stopped to bivouac only after crossing the Broad River. Morgan then paused to regroup, dispatch the prisoners to Virginia under militia escort, and send a report to Greene, who received Morgan’s report on 23 January 1781;

by that point, Morgan’s light corps had crossed the Catawba River at Sherrald’s Ford, north of Charlotte. Morgan had deliberately taken a circuitous route northwest from the Cowpens to Gilbert Town (present-day Rutherfordton, North Carolina) before turning east to Sherrald’s Ford—a forced march of 100 miles in 5 days. Morgan positioned militia detachments to watch the fords for the expected British pursuit and waited for Greene’s response.Morgan’s unexpected victory at Cowpens upset the strategic calculus for both Greene and Cornwallis. Greene was naturally pleased with Morgan’s victory. Yet Greene’s army was dangerously dispersed, and Cornwallis’s remaining army was larger than Morgan’s corps. Greene briefly considered regrouping to attack Ninety Six, but he abandoned the idea after conferring with Morgan at Sherrald’s Ford. Morgan had received only Maj. Gen. William Lee Davidson’s 700 North Carolina militiamen as reinforcements—good troops, but not enough to guard all fording points of the Catawba. Moreover, Greene’s principal logistics base at Salisbury lay only 40 miles to the northeast, and presented a tempting target for Cornwallis’s hungry redcoats. Finally, Greene believed Cornwallis might try to trap Greene’s army against that of Benedict Arnold (now a British brigadier general) advancing from eastern Virginia. Greene thus ordered his army to conduct a strategic withdrawal northeast toward Virginia starting on 30 January 1781—beginning with the evacuation of the tons of food, forage, and ordnance stores at Salisbury. Greene then ordered Brig. Gen. Isaac Huger to march his Continental troops and logistics trains from Cheraw to support the Salisbury withdrawal. Greene lastly directed Morgan to continue screening the Catawba fords, fighting if necessary to cover the Salisbury withdrawal without exposing the light troops to heavy losses. Greene characteristically looked beyond the immediate risk to his divided army and saw the possibility of inflicting a strategic defeat on Cornwallis’s overextended army: “It is necessary we should take every possible precaution to guard against misfortune. But I am not without hopes of ruining Lord Cornwallis if he persists in his mad scheme of pushing through the Country and it is my earnest desire to form a junction as soon as possible for this purpose.”

In the interim, Cornwallis prepared to resume his “mad scheme” after the arrival of Maj. Gen. Alexander Leslie’s brigade of 1,200 soldiers from Virginia’s Tidewater, giving Cornwallis a strength of about 2,500. Cornwallis reported the Cowpens disaster to Clinton in New York but carefully omitted his abandonment of the pacification strategy. He instead shared his plans—albeit only with Lord George Germain in London—to destroy Greene’s army and then occupy North Carolina. Cornwallis used his mounted scouts to gather intelligence about the American dispositions, but he failed to use his skilled Royal Engineer officers to survey roads and river crossings. Cornwallis blundered by marching to the presumably shallower fords on the upper Broad River beginning on 18 January 1781. The British instead found the upper Broad was deeper than expected, further delaying the army’s slow movement on muddy piedmont roads. Cornwallis’s army straggled into Ramsour’s Mill on 25 January to rest and forage. By then, loyalist scouts had located Morgan’s troops about 20 miles away, closely guarding the main fords on the east branch of the Catawba River. Cornwallis then made an unorthodox decision to reset the odds in his favor: The train of wagons that now attended [the army] met with great obstacles on the march, which considerably impeded the progress of the army. On the 25th, a halt was made . . . for the purpose of destroying all the baggage and carriages, except such that was absolutely necessary. Earl Cornwallis reduced the size and quantity of his own baggage, and this laudable example was followed by . . . other officers under his command. After adopting this measure, so necessary for the prosecution of offensive operations, the army proceeded towards the Catawba.Cornwallis’s attempt to improve his mobility by reducing his army’s wagons also meant the army had to stop more frequently to gather forage and provisions. He also found the army was slowed further by

a group of ill soldiers, American prisoners, and more women than those authorized “on the strength” of individual regiments. Heavy rains hindered British movements, and it reached Beattie’s Ford on 28 January only to find the Catawba River flooded and impassable. Cornwallis’s troops used the enforced halt to forage, care for animals, and repair worn clothing and equipment.Cornwallis judged the river level low enough to attempt a surprise crossing at the lightly defended Cowan’s Ford on 1 February 1781, aided by a diversionary attack at Beattie’s Ford by Lt. Col. James Webster’s brigade. Cornwallis and Leslie both were unhorsed during the process, and many redcoats died from drowning or gunfire. The surviving British troops drove off the demoralized Carolina militiamen, and Davidson suffered a mortal wound. Cornwallis’s crossing compelled Morgan to consolidate his remaining detachments and run toward Greene’s army. Cornwallis’s gambit thus succeeded, but at the cost of a hundred more dead or injured, and Morgan’s army was still on the loose. Tarleton’s troopers followed the American trail and overran some laggard rebel militiamen at Torrence’s Tavern. Tarleton noted with satisfaction that word of the skirmish “diffused such a terror among the inhabitants, that the King’s troops passed through the most hostile part of North Carolina without a shot from the militia.” Cornwallis, however, admonished Tarleton for allowing his troopers to plunder wagons and nearby houses instead of continuing the pursuit. While the Tory dragoons were thus engaged, Morgan safely reached Salisbury despite a heavy rainstorm (Map 4).Greene, meanwhile, had adjusted his strategic dispositions by ordering Davie’s quartermasters to load workshops and movable stores from Salisbury. On 2 February, the wagon train marched to rendezvous with the prepositioned bateaux flotilla at Trading Ford on the Yadkin River. After seeing the wagon train on its way, Greene sent messages redirecting General Huger and Colonel Lee to a new rendezvous point at Guilford Courthouse. Tarleton’s advanced guard reached Salisbury on 3 February. The main body paused there to gather the leftover supplies while Brig. Gen. Charles O’Hara’s Brigade of Guards continued the pursuit. O’Hara’s guards finally

reached Trading Ford after hours in mud and rain, only to find a handful of abandoned wagons and an enemy militia patrol watching the Yadkin River. With no boats and another flooded river to his front, Cornwallis rested his army until he found a suitable crossing point upstream.Greene sent his main body on from Trading Ford to Guilford Courthouse while he and a small covering detachment monitored British movements. When Greene saw the British army break camp and march upstream, he correctly assumed Cornwallis was continuing his pursuit. Despite the horrid weather and lack of militia reinforcements, Greene was cautiously optimistic: How is it possible an army circumstanced as ours is, can make head against one organized and equipped as Lord Cornwallises is...It is not improbable from Lord Cornwallises pushing disposition, and the contempt he has for our Army, we may precipitate him into some capital misfortune. . . . If Lord Cornwallis knows his true interest he will pursue our army. If he can disperse that, he compleats the reduction of the State; and without that he will do nothing to effect. Cornwallis’s troops crossed the ebbing Yadkin on 7 February 1781 at Shallow Ford, by which point Greene’s army was 25 miles away at Guilford Courthouse. Greene held a council of war there on 9 February, and his officers unanimously recommended that the army avoid fighting until reinforced. Greene already had decided as much, and reorganized the flying army with Washington’s Legionary Corps, Lee’s 2d Partisan Corps, Lt. Col. John Eager Howard’s provisional battalion, and Maj. David Campbell’s Virginia riflemen—780 troops in total—to screen the withdrawal. Greene selected Col. Otho Holland Williams of the 6th Maryland to replace Morgan, who was stricken with debilitating rheumatism and piles (hemorrhoids).

Greene’s lumbering supply trains, field guns, and their Continental infantry escort rolled from Guilford Courthouse on 10 February toward the lower fords of the Dan River at Irwin’s and Boyd’s Ferries (at today’s South Boston, Virginia). Williams’s flying army marched westward to gain contact with the British and led them northward toward Dix’s Ferry on the upper Dan—thereby distracting Cornwallis from the movement of the main body. American and loyalist dragoons clashed at Bruce’s Mill, only 7 miles from Guilford Courthouse. The Americans ended the skirmish by tearing planks from a bridge spanning Reedy Fork Creek, forcing Tarleton’s dragoons on a costly detour while Williams’s soldiers force marched toward Dix’s Ferry. From 11 to 13 February, Cornwallis relentlessly drove his army after the American light troops, hindered by hasty obstacles and harassing attacks by local rebel militiamen. Sgt. Maj. William Seymour of the Delaware Regiment later described the withdrawal:On the eighth instant [8 February], we marched from here, General Greene’s army taking one road and the light troops another. . . . This day we received intelligence that the British Army was advancing very close in our rear. . . . We marched . . . on the ninth inst., taking the road towards Dan River, which we reached on the fourteenth, after a march of two hundred and fifty miles from . . . our encampment at Pacolet River . . . we marched for the most part both day and night, the main of the British being close in our rear, so that we had not scarce time to cook our victuals, their whole attention being on our light troops. In the meantime, Greene’s troops and camp followers crossed the Dan River on light boats while engineers used the bateaux to carry across the heavy wagons and cannons. The army finished its movement by midday on 14 February, prompting Greene to send a

message to Williams ordering him to break contact and withdraw to Boyd’s Ferry. Williams’s corps outdistanced the pursuing British and safely crossed by torchlight at Boyd’s Ferry, with Greene, Williams, and Lee in the last boats. Tarleton’s advance guard reached Irwin’s Ferry early on 15 February, only to find “some works evacuated, which had been constructed to cover the retreat of the enemy, who six hours before had finished their passage, and were then encamped on the opposite bank. Every measure of the Americans, during their march from the Catawba to Virginia, was judiciously designed and vigorously executed.”While the American troops rested from their exertions, General Greene implemented measures to retain the initiative. He believed Cornwallis had three possible options: move to the proloyalist Hillsborough region for recruits and supplies; continue the pursuit into Virginia; or establish communications with General Arnold’s army via the Roanoke River at Halifax, North Carolina. Greene sent Steuben to prevent Arnold’s army from leaving Portsmouth, Virginia, and Kosciusko to fortify Halifax. Greene urged Governor Thomas Jefferson of Virginia and Governor Abner Nash of North Carolina to call out their available alarm militia and state line units to reinforce the Continentals. Greene quickly reassessed his campaign plan after learning Cornwallis’s army was regrouping in North Carolina, as he noted to Governor Jefferson:When the Enemy first took their departure from the Dan they had every prospect of great reinforcements from the Tories of Carolina . . . if they were permitted to roam at large in the State that it would indubitably impress the idea of Conquest upon the Minds of the disaffected . . . and perhaps occasion those . . . to take an active and decisive part against us. I instantly determined . . . to advance into the state. . . . It was necessary to convince the Carolinians that they were not conquered and by affording immediate protection . . . engage the continuance of their confidence and friendship.
