text: Although he knew the army needed time to regroup, Greene realized the same respite would give Cornwallis time to reorganize and recruit loyalist reinforcements. Greene knew a quick resumption of active operations by his Continentals would both boost the morale of patriot militiamen and demonstrate Cornwallis’s failures to loyalist sympathizers. Greene thus badgered Governors Jefferson and Nash for supplies, fresh mounted troops, and additional light infantry. Greene also wrote to General Steuben in Virginia to urge the rapid shipment of new muskets, cartridge boxes, and ordnance stores to arm the new troops. Cornwallis, meanwhile, had withdrawn to Hillsborough, North Carolina, where he expected to receive loyalist reinforcements and provisions. British General O’Hara wrote disgustedly about the lackluster response by local Tories: “The novelty of a camp in the backwoods of America more than any other cause brought several people to stare at us. Their curiosity once satisfied, they returned to their homes.” Contrary to O’Hara’s complaint, a significant number of loyalists supported Commissary Charles Stedman as wagoners and cattle drivers. Stedman organized foraging detachments to confiscate livestock and provisions from the locals—necessary measures that further alienated many otherwise sympathetic Americans. Cornwallis’s scouts detected the arrival of the rebel militia reinforcements but missed the reentry of Lee’s 2d Partisan Corps and recently promoted Brig. Gen. Andrew Pickens’s militia regiment into North Carolina—the first movement of Greene’s counteroffensive. Several hundred loyalist recruits also joined Cornwallis at Hillsborough, who sent them to train with Tarleton’s Legion at Wetzell’s Mill on Reedy Fork Creek—a popular reprovisioning spot for both armies. The uptick in enemy movements prompted Colonel Lee to set ambushes for isolated loyalist patrols. On 25 February, a column of new loyalist recruits under Lt. Col. John Pyle unwittingly mistook Lee’s green-jacketed dragoons for Tarleton’s Legion troopers. Before Lee could tell the encircled and defenseless Tories to lay down their arms, an exchange of gunfire

precipitated a bloody and one-sided melee. The hardened Continental and patriot troops quickly killed 90 and captured 250 of the hapless Tories—while the few who escaped spread the word of what became known as “Pyle’s Hacking Match.” The destruction of Pyle’s regiment further depressed loyalist spirits and their willingness to support the British army openly.

Greene received enough reinforcements—roughly 1,600 Virginia State Line infantry and militia rifle units—to recross his main force into North Carolina on 23 February 1781. Greene replicated his earlier Cowpens operational approach by splitting heavy and light troops (flying army), thereby confusing Cornwallis while reducing the demand for provisions and fodder in a single district. After several days of feinting and skirmishing, Cornwallis tried to trap Colonel Williams’s flying army near Wetzell’s Mill, where it was “posted carelessly at separate plantations for the convenience of subsisting.” Cornwallis dispatched Colonel Webster’s reinforced brigade of 1,200 troops: three infantry regiments, Tarleton’s Legion, and a company each of Guards light infantry and Ansbach jaegers (riflemen). Williams’s flying army consisted of Lee’s 2d Partisan Corps, Pickens’s South Carolina militia regiment, three North Carolina militia companies, and a battalion of Virginia riflemen—about 700 troops. With Tarleton’s Legion in the vanguard, Webster’s brigade marched from their camp early on 6 March 1781 to catch the Americans in their bedrolls. The British advance was concealed by fog, but Lee’s pickets detected the enemy movement and gave the alarm. Williams immediately deployed his light infantry and militia to delay Webster’s advance while the Continentals and dragoons took up firing positions on the far side of Reedy Fork Creek. Lee’s light infantry drove back the initial attack, buying time for the American light troops to wade the creek. Webster riposted by sending his light infantry to cross upstream, but they were blocked in turn

by Colonel Washington’s 3d Legionary Corps, which screened Williams’s withdrawal back to Greene’s bivouac site. Each side lost about thirty casualties, but Cornwallis’s troops had fumbled an opportunity to encircle and destroy many irreplaceable Continentals. Williams’s near destruction reinforced Greene’s caution, and the British found American security tighter than before. Greene did not publicly criticize Williams after the battle, but Pickens’s militiamen were incensed at Williams’s blunder and most deserted for home. Greene was compelled to release Pickens to regroup his militia in South Carolina to keep the local loyalists in check. The quick American reaction, however, reflected the progress made by Greene and his officers in improving the combat effectiveness of the force.

The arrival of two brigades of 1,500 North Carolina militiamen and two brigades of 1,200 Virginia state line soldiers soon offset Pickens’s departure. Greene also received fresh Continental forces to reinforce the battle-tested but understrength 1st Maryland, led by Col. John Gunby. The newly recruited 2d Maryland Regiment, commanded by Lt. Col. Benjamin Ford, was brigaded with the 1st Maryland under the command of Colonel Williams. The Virginia Brigade, commanded by Brig. Gen. Isaac Huger, joined up with the 1st Virginia Regiment under Col. John Green and the 2d Virginia Regiment under Lt. Col. Samuel Hawes. Greene reorganized his army, creating two corps of observation by attaching light infantry and rifle companies to Washington’s Legionary Corps and Lee’s Partisan Corps, with each expected “to attend to the enemies movements upon the left with Washington on the right . . . to give the enemy all the annoyance in your power, and each to report to Head Quarters.” With the fresh reinforcements, Greene assessed that: Our force was much more respectable that it had been, and that there was a much greater probability of its

declining than increasing, and that there would be the greatest difficulty in subsisting it long in the field in this exhausted Country, I took the resolution of attacking the Enemy without loss of time . . . being persuaded that if we were successful it would prove ruinous to the enemy, and if otherwise, it would only prove a partial evil to us.Greene’s army left its camp on the Haw River on 12 March and took two days to march 22 miles to Guilford Courthouse. Greene’s stated intent was to attack Cornwallis but, mindful of the British preference for surprise attacks, he prepared his command for battle by rehearsing on defensible terrain west of Guilford Courthouse. He also used the corps of observation to ensure security and reduce the risk of loss by sending his wagon train and camp followers to Speedwell Ironworks on Reedy Fork Creek. Meanwhile, Cornwallis struggled to keep his army fed and prepared for action. His problems stemmed from the decision to destroy the army’s wagon train just after the battle at Cowpens. American efforts had stripped provisions and livestock from local Tories, and so the British had to devote most of their time to foraging. Consequently, Stedman’s commissaries could gather only 4 ounces each of cornmeal and meat per day—a modicum of the standard daily ration of a pound of bread and a pound of beef or three-quarters of a pound of salt pork. The absence of rum or spirits further depressed morale in Cornwallis’s army, leading many redcoats to sneak from camp to loot houses for liquor. By 14 March, Cornwallis’s army was reduced to taking provisions from the pacifistic Quakers at the Deep River Meeting House, 12 miles from Guilford Courthouse. On that same day, Cornwallis’s scouts reported Greene’s location, prompting a desperate Cornwallis to plan an attack the following day—before his army ran out of supplies. At 0530 on 15 March 1781, Tarleton’s Legion led the advance up the New Garden Road toward Guilford Courthouse while the supply and hospital echelon marched to safety near Bell’s Mills on the Deep River.Greene screened his battle position by positioning Lee’s corps of observation—150 dragoons and mounted light infantry, a company

each of Continental light infantry and Virginia riflemen—at the New Garden Meeting House. The settlement lay along Cornwallis’s expected route of march along the New Garden Road. Lee’s scouts immediately detected the British movements and kept Greene apprised of Cornwallis’s advance. By contrast, Tarleton’s light troops were surprised when Lee’s skirmishers near the meeting house opened fire. During the next two hours, the provincial and American light forces skirmished on both sides of the meeting house. Casualties on both sides were fewer than fifty killed and wounded, but Lee’s troops had skillfully disrupted the British advance while giving Greene time to finish deploying his forces.Greene used the time wisely by feeding his soldiers and exhorting them as they filed into line of battle. Greene did not record a detailed battle plan, but his dispositions indicate he planned a delaying defense, trading space for time without exposing his Continentals to needless risk (Map 5). Earlier, Morgan had recommended a three-line deployment, like that at Cowpens, but with additional light troops to anchor the flanks. Greene broadly followed Morgan’s suggestions, starting by placing Brig. Gen. Thomas Eaton’s and Brig. Gen. John Butler’s North Carolina brigades behind a fence that offered good fields of fire toward the oncoming enemy force. Greene then placed the Virginia brigades on the reverse western slope of Hunting Creek. He posted Brig. Gen. Robert Lawson to the north of New Garden Road and Brig. Gen. Edward Stevens to the south. Greene then arrayed the four Continental regiments atop high ground overlooking Hunting Creek—a location close to Reedy Fork Road, which led to the field trains at Speedwell Ironworks. Greene lastly positioned Washington’s corps of observation on the North Carolina right flank and Lee’s corps protecting the left (southern) flank. Greene’s plan deviated in other critical details from Morgan’s recommendations. First, Greene did not deploy skirmishers before the North Carolina militia line to attrit and disrupt the British advance. Second, Greene arrayed his lines beyond mutual supporting distance, leaving each vulnerable to defeat in detail. Third, Greene ordered the North Carolina brigades to fire two shots and withdraw but gave no further follow-on orders. Lastly, Greene stayed in the

third line while the battle unfolded, leaving the militia troops without an overall commander to coordinate their actions. Cornwallis’s army deployed into line of battle near the Hoskins farmstead under cover of their 3-pounder guns. The two Continental Map 5

6-pounders supporting the North Carolina line returned fire, an exchange that caused few casualties but unnerved many North Carolina militiamen. Cornwallis positioned Colonel Webster’s brigade of the 23d and 33d Foot on the left side of the New Garden Road, with General Leslie’s brigade of the 71st Foot (Highlanders) and the German Regiment Von Bose deployed to the right. Cornwallis split General O’Hara’s Brigade of Guards, placing the 1st Battalion of Guards on the right in support and the 2d Battalion of Guards on the left. Cornwallis retained the individual Guards Light Infantry, Grenadiers, and German jaeger companies, and Tarleton’s dragoons in reserve, instead of using them for reconnaissance or skirmishing tasks. Cornwallis opened the battle shortly after noon by launching a frontal assault on the North Carolina militia line.Greene’s delaying defense began when the riflemen on both flanks engaged the enemy officers with long-range fire. Some nervous North Carolinians ignored their orders to fire in volleys and took individual shots at the advancing redcoats. The British tactical response to militia was an advance at a 120-paces-per-minute quick step with leveled bayonets. The intent was to close into hand-to-hand fighting range before the enemy could reload, but Webster’s troops were delayed by having to hop fences and cross sodden fields. Eaton’s North Carolinians let off a devastating volley when the enemy troops were about 50 yards from the last fence. Webster’s troops responded with an immediate volley and bayonet charge that reached the enemy militia line before many rebels could reload. Leslie erred by ordering his regiments to alternate fire and movement, thereby giving many of Butler’s North Carolinians time to fire a third volley in the faces of the British and German troops. Most of the Carolina troops ran for their lives, but some stood with their officers and fought with clubbed muskets and knives. Webster’s units continued eastward through the shattered North Carolina line, but the terrain and pockets of resistance split his brigade line. Cornwallis and O’Hara responded by pushing the 2d Guards and light infantry companies into support of Webster’s running engagement with Washington’s corps of observation. To the south, some North Carolinians fell in with Lee’s corps of observation on the American left to fight a

delaying action against the Regiment Von Bose and the 1st Guards. Cornwallis’s initial attack broke the North Carolinian line, but at the cost of heavy casualties and the dispersion of his army.The sounds of battle and the sight of running North Carolinians warned the Virginia troops of the British advance. The Virginia brigades fought better, as they had been well trained by the ex-Continental officers and soldiers in their ranks. Lawson’s brigade fought stubbornly until it was hit by a counterstroke from the Guards Light Infantry company and the 33d Foot—as later described by Maj. St. George Tucker: “This threw the militia into such confusion. . . . Holcombe’s regiment and ours instantly broke off without firing a single gun and dispersed like a flock of sheep frightened by dogs.” Even then, many of Lawson’s officers rallied squads and platoons that maintained “an irregular kind of skirmishing with the British.” Webster’s brigade eventually broke through Lawson’s scattered regiments, but only at a high cost in casualties and expended ammunition. Meanwhile, Washington’s corps of observation continued a fighting withdrawal back to protect the Continental right flank on the third line.On the southern half of the battlefield, Stevens’s brigade of 750 soldiers fought hard to avenge their humiliating defeat at Camden. The odds were too great, and many Virginians ran after Stevens fell with a shattered femur in the middle of a melee with bayonets and clubbed muskets. Even then, several Virginian companies and platoons remained intact to fall in with Lee’s corps of observation. Stevens’s stand cost the British heavily in casualties and slowed the momentum of their advance toward the Continental main line.General O’Hara fell wounded at the second line, and Cornwallis narrowly escaped capture after his horse was shot from under him. Webster pushed through the maelstrom with the 33d Foot and three light infantry companies to reach the open area by Hunting Creek—where he ordered a frontal attack on what he assumed was a single Continental regiment and the 6-pounder section near the Salisbury Road. Webster’s troops were shocked as they took fire from two unbloodied Virginia Continental

regiments and their supporting artillery. The British troops recoiled from the American fire to shelter in the woods west of the creek. Webster’s soldiers barely had reached cover when O’Hara and the 2d Guards reached the creek edge near the road. The British again launched an immediate attack against the left flank of the Continental line. The 2d Guards had better luck as they rolled up the right flank of the poorly positioned 2d Maryland and its supporting “Battle of Guildford, Fought on the 15th of March 1781,” William Faden, London, 1787  (Library of Congress Geography and Map Division)

gun section. The 2d Guards were surprised in turn by a counterattack from the veteran 1st Maryland Continentals and Washington’s dragoons. A brutal close-range fight occurred between the redcoats and the Continental infantry and dragoons. The Americans came close to overwhelming the 2d Guards but instead were driven off by salvos of grapeshot directed by Cornwallis personally. Cornwallis’s appearance with the artillery and the concurrent arrival of the 23d Foot and Highlanders convinced Greene it was time to save his Continentals to fight another day. Greene ordered General Huger’s Virginia Continental Brigade to screen the withdrawal. Greene also ordered the surviving Continental gunners to leave their 6-pounder guns on the battlefield as their horses had been wounded or killed. Elements of the 23d, 71st, and Tarleton’s Legion attempted a pursuit, but the Virginia Continentals held the enemy troops at bay, allowing Greene’s army to withdraw safely toward Speedwell Ironworks.However, fighting continued south of Salisbury Road between scattered North Carolina and Virginia detachments, Lee’s corps of observation, and the 1st Battalion of Guards. The wooded terrain disordered the redcoats, allowing militia skirmishers and Lee’s light troops to inflict heavy casualties. The 1st Guards were saved from destruction only by the timely intervention of the Regiment Von Bose, which formed a hollow square to present its bayonets against the American attackers. The British commanders rallied their troops and resumed fighting alongside the Regiment Von Bose. Soon thereafter, Lee unexpectedly broke contact and withdrew toward the courthouse—just as Tarleton led a troop of his dragoons with drawn sabers into the North Carolina and Virginia militiamen. Many American militiamen were cut down, and others scattered into the trees to escape. One American managed to maim Tarleton’s right hand with a lucky rifle shot before the Legion ended its pursuit. As the Continental rear guard marched north toward Speedwell Ironworks, Cornwallis rallied his units at the courthouse, thus ending the battle after three hours of fighting. The weather after the battle turned cool and rainy, but the surviving American troops enjoyed the shelter and double rations at the Speedwell Ironworks camp.

By contrast, the hungry and tired British soldiers had no means of shelter from the storm because of Cornwallis’s earlier decision to destroy the excess wagons and baggage. The hapless wounded were left unattended on the battlefield overnight, and many consequently died from shock and exposure.What were the results of the battle? Greene’s army of 4,400 Continentals and militia lost 79 dead, 184 wounded, and 1,046 missing in action (most of whom were militiamen who left the battlefield and went home), along with four cannons and an indeterminate number of abandoned firearms. Greene expressed his satisfaction with the outcome, as his army had inflicted disproportionately heavy losses on the enemy. He noted: “The battle was long, obstinate and bloody. . . . But the enemy have been so soundly beaten, that they dare not move towards us. . . . Except the ground and the Artillery they have gained no advantage, on the contrary they are a little short of being ruined.” Greene’s assessment was correct, as Cornwallis’s army of 1,900 soldiers had suffered a debilitating 28 percent loss rate: 93 dead, 413 wounded, and 26 missing in action. Leader losses were especially heavy, with fourteen killed and thirteen wounded. Webster and two junior officers died of their wounds. Under a flag of truce, the British and the Americans agreed to collectively evacuate the wounded to field hospitals at the Hoskins farmstead and New Garden Meeting House, while soldiers and locals interred the dead in common graves. Cornwallis rested his troops for two days at the courthouse before leaving his seriously wounded at New Garden Meeting House and returning to Bell’s Mill. Once there, Cornwallis issued a proclamation of victory, offered parole to surrendering rebels, and elicited loyalist recruits. Cornwallis wryly noted the tepid response in his battle report: “Many of the inhabitants rode into camp, shook me by the hand, said they were glad to see us, and to hear that we had beat Greene, and then rode home again.” Cornwallis eventually marched his army to Wilmington, North Carolina, after he realized he could no longer sustain his army in the increasingly hostile and barren region. Greene followed the British army to the Deep River Meeting House, where “the want of provisions and a considerable part of

the Virginia Militias time being expired, will prevent our further pursuit.” Greene camped his army and sent out scouts and spies to track Cornwallis, whom he correctly assumed would march through Cross Creek to Wilmington.

While his army rested and regrouped, Greene opted for another change in his campaign plan:[R]emote from reinforcements, inferior to the enemy in numbers and no prospec[t] of support I am at a loss what is best to be done. . . . In this critical and distressing situation I am determined to carry the War immediately into South Carolina. The Enemy will be obliged to follow us or give up their posts in the State. If the former takes place it will draw the War out of [North Carolina]. . . . If they leave their posts to fall they must lose more there then they can gain here. . . . All things considered I think the movement is warranted by the soundest reasons both political and military.Greene recognized the risk of leaving Cornwallis to march unimpeded into Virginia; he also knew that Cornwallis could remain in North Carolina as well. Greene, however, judged the opportunity to eliminate British outposts in the Carolinas as worth the risk—especially because Washington could send reinforcements more easily to Virginia than to the Carolinas. This last point was borne out by the October 1780 landing of General Arnold and 2,000 British troops at Portsmouth, Virginia. Virginia levies under Brig. Gen. Peter Muhlenberg contained the British until Steuben and 1,200 reinforcements under the command of Maj. Gen. Marie-Joseph Paul Yves Roch Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette, arrived in support. Greene decided to move southward in late March 1781, well before he knew Cornwallis’s intentions, yet he hedged his bets

by resting his army at the Deep River until early April. Greene used his time there writing letters to Congress in Philadelphia; Steuben and Jefferson in Virginia; and other officials to obtain fresh levies, supplies, and weapons to replace those lost during the 1781 Carolinas campaign. Cornwallis rested his battered army at Wilmington while he rethought his campaign plans. Instead of resuming his original strategic task of pacifying South Carolina, Cornwallis instead marched his army toward Virginia on 25 April 1781. Once there, Cornwallis fought several engagements but failed to attain his goal of blocking reinforcements and supplies to Greene’s army. Cornwallis entrenched his exhausted army at Yorktown in late September 1781, where a joint Franco-American force compelled his surrender on 19 October 1781. Yorktown was in the future, however, and the present remained uncertain. In the interim, Greene could only advise Governor Jefferson and the Continental forces defending Virginia, while keeping his strategic focus on regaining control of the Carolinas.

Greene marched southward on 6 April, with the expectation that  supplies and reinforcements would soon follow. Greene’s army had shrunk in the interim with the departure of North Carolina alarm militia and Virginia volunteers. He commanded only the Virginia and Maryland Continental brigades, Capt. Robert Kirkwood’s Continental Delaware light infantry company, Washington’s dragoons, and a Continental artillery detachment under Col. Charles Harrison—about 1,500 soldiers. The Americans faced about 5,200 regular and provincial troops and several hundred loyalist volunteers and alarm militia, all under the overall command of Colonel Rawdon. Rawdon’s forces were scattered in garrisons at Ninety Six, Camden, and small outposts along the interior lines of communications—thus vulnerable to defeat in detail.Freed and enslaved Black soldiers augmented the British numbers, but a lack of clear policy guidance from London hindered the Crown forces’ ability to make use of this potential

volunteer pool. Instead, commanders had to proceed carefully lest they provoke a rebellion among the freed Black contingents or lose the support of slave-holding loyalists. In 1779, Sir Henry Clinton had issued a proclamation that promised freedom to rebel-owned enslaved people who entered British lines—but deliberately excluded South Carolina from its remit to avoid losing the manpower necessary to raise food crops on loyalists’ plantations. Enslaved people fleeing from patriot owners still were welcomed and given paid employment as artisans and teamsters supporting the war effort. British commanders also employed enslaved Black laborers to help fortify places like Camden and Ninety Six. The White population largely balked at arming Black people, aside from a few temporary measures taken by British and loyalist officers facing rebel insurgent attacks on isolated posts. A notable exception was the Continental Army, which allowed for the enlistment of free Black men, even in southern regiments. Black Continentals, however, faced the extra risk of being forcibly enslaved if taken prisoner by the British.By 19 April 1781, Greene’s little army was camped atop Hobkirk Hill, a sandy ridge astride the Great Waxhaws Road north of Camden. Greene positioned his army there to fix Rawdon’s garrison at Logtown—a cluster of log houses guarding the northern approaches to Camden—and planned to use militia detachments to seize the crossing points of the Wateree and Lynches Rivers. Greene wrote to Pickens, Sumter, and Marion about his plan and asked for their cooperation. Pickens and Marion agreed to support the plan, although many of their soldiers were committed elsewhere. Sumter, by contrast, rebuffed Greene’s request, forcing Greene to ask for militia troops from North Carolina and Virginia instead. Sumter’s refusal owed much to his bruised ego, as Greene had appointed Morgan instead of him to command the flying army. Further offense came in January when Greene undiplomatically implied Sumter’s troops were motivated by “plunder and depredation.” Greene’s assertions largely were correct, as evidenced by Sumter’s ill-conceived offensive below Camden in early 1781. His failed attack on Fort Granby was motivated by the promise of loot, and the capture and loss of booty

from Big Savannah aroused suspicions of treachery among Sumter’s troops. Sumter then tried to enlist men into South Carolina state dragoons by offering confiscated enslaved people as bounty—an initiative known as “Sumter’s Law.” Greene reluctantly approved the measure, fearing correctly that Sumter’s bounty would further stimulate looting and tit-for-tat Whig and Tory reprisals. Sumter subsequently cooperated only when he saw the advantage to his own goals, despite Greene’s efforts at reconciliation. Meanwhile, Rawdon’s energies were consumed by securing Camden, Ninety Six and the vulnerable supply lines with Charleston. He thwarted several partisan attacks but at the cost of tying up reinforcements intended for Cornwallis’s army. Tory sympathizers reported Greene’s position accurately, allowing Rawdon to consider a spoiling attack on the American army at Hobkirk Hill. (See Map 6.) Greene expected an enemy counterstroke and positioned his regiments and guns overlooking the open areas along the Waxhaws Road behind a strong skirmish line. Greene also sent Captain Kirkwood’s Delaware light infantry to probe the British defenses. Kirkwood’s skirmishers successfully seized Logtown, though they found Camden itself strongly fortified.Meanwhile, Rawdon decided to strike after receiving intelligence that Greene was temporarily vulnerable with detachments from the main body—which included Lee and Marion—attacking Fort Watson. On 25 April 1781, Rawdon marched his raiding force quietly up the wooded eastern side of Hobkirk Hill by skirting Pine Tree Creek. Alert American pickets raised the alarm, prompting Kirkwood to deploy his light infantry as skirmishers—which bought time for the Continental officers to gather their soldiers from the camp and deploy for combat. Greene arrayed his four Continental regiments—the 1st and 2d Maryland Regiments on the left and the 4th and 5th Virginia Regiments on the right—facing southward, with the field guns and a security detachment in support. Lastly, Greene held Colonel Washington’s light Continental dragoons and a North Carolina militia battalion in reserve. Greene’s army numbered roughly 1,300 Continentals and 250 militiamen, whereas Rawdon led perhaps 900 troops: the regular 63d Foot, the provincials

of the Volunteers of Ireland and the King’s American Regiment, the New York Volunteers, and a troop of the New York Dragoons. The Volunteers were a unique organization, organized by Rawdon in 1777 from Irish immigrants and Continental deserters, whose desire to serve with fellow Catholic Irishmen outweighed their normal anti-British attitudes. The regiment fought so well in the north that the British government added it to the permanent army list as the 2d American Regiment in May 1779.The Continental artillery opened the battle by raking the British columns with grapeshot while Greene ordered a bayonet charge and flanking attack by Washington’s squadron. The artillery fire surprised Rawdon, who tardily deployed his regiments from column into line to meet the Continental advance. The American attack inflicted heavy casualties and seemed on the point of success when the veteran 1st Maryland unaccountably fell apart, giving Rawdon an opening to launch a countercharge. The disorder spread to all but the 5th Virginia, which formed a wall of bayonets to protect the disorganized withdrawal of the field guns and remaining infantry. Thus covered, Greene pulled his army back to regroup near the old Camden battlefield. Left behind on the battlefield were 19 dead, 113 wounded, and 138 missing, whereas Rawdon incurred 38 dead, 177 wounded, and 43 missing. Greene heaped blame on Colonel Gunby of the 1st Maryland for failing to control his unit, while ignoring Colonel Washington’s failure to employ his dragoons effectively. Washington inexplicably had led his regiment on a wide circuit. Instead of falling on the rear of Rawdon’s infantry, the Continental troopers scooped up rear echelon troops near Logtown. Greene, however, also failed to admit his own role in initiating a meeting engagement instead of defending in place with his superior numbers and firepower. After some reflection, Greene realized the battle had not changed the overall strategic situation: “This repulse, if such it may be called, will make no alteration in our general plan of operations.” Rawdon soon arrived at that same conclusion after he failed to fix and attack Greene’s army after its withdrawal.

In the interim, Lee’s legion and Marion’s partisans surrounded Fort Watson, which lay on the British supply line between Camden and Charleston. The Americans found the enemy had skillfully fortified the top of a 22-foot-high Santee tribal burial mound. After a plan to obtain a field gun from Greene went awry, Lt. Col. Hezekiah Maham, Marion’s dragoon commander, orchestrated the building of a 30-foot-tall siege tower of logs under the cover of darkness. Riflemen atop the “Maham Tower” and Continentals at the base shot down several defenders at dawn on 23 April 1781, thereby allowing a team to begin breaching the fort—which compelled the wounded British commander to surrender. The loss of Fort Watson and the proximity of Greene’s army convinced Rawdon that he could not remain at Camden any longer. On 27 April 1781, Rawdon evacuated the garrison. He relocated willing loyalist supporters and their households and movable stores approximately 100 miles southeastward to Monck’s Corner. The evacuation emboldened the Whig militia and convinced many Tory The Battle of Hobkirk’s Hill, F. C. Yohn, 1898 (New York Public Library)

sympathizers to seek protection by joining the patriot side. Many hardcore loyalists continued to fight alone, but Sumter considered their resistance “little more than a nuisance and more than offset by the number of men in the area who joined the Whigs.”Rawdon’s evacuation of Camden set off a cascade of further British reverses. Lee and Marion’s combined light force captured Orangeburg and cut the Congaree River line by seizing Forts Motte and Granby—yielding some 215 British and 400 loyalist prisoners, plus dozens of muskets and wagonloads of valuable supplies. Lt. Col. Nisbet Balfour, the British commander at Charleston, panicked and evacuated Georgetown before Lee and Marion could assault the seaport town. The evacuation of Camden and the closing of the Congaree to boat traffic left Ninety Six and Augusta isolated in enemy-controlled territory. On 10 May 1781, Rawdon sent orders to Lt. Col. John Harris Cruger at Ninety Six to withdraw his garrison and movable stores to reinforce the Augusta garrison. A patriot militia patrol scooped up the loyalist couriers, leaving Cruger ignorant of his dangerous isolation. Greene had expected Rawdon to order an evacuation, so he reacted to the new intelligence by marching to lay siege to Ninety Six. To keep Rawdon distracted, Greene dispatched Lee’s partisan corps to cooperate with Pickens and Col. Elijah Clarke of Georgia in attacking British-held Augusta—which surrendered on 6 June 1781.Greene’s army consisted of two Maryland and two Virginia Continental regiments, a North Carolina and Continental light infantry company each, and three 6-pounder gun sections—about 984 troops. Greene’s corps outnumbered Cruger’s garrison of 350 New York and New Jersey provincials and 200 Carolina loyalists, but Cruger’s troops had the advantage of fighting from fortifications. The centerpiece of the defense was the star fort—laid out by Cornwallis’s engineer, Lt. Henry Haldane, in mid-1781—built by work parties of soldiers and conscripted enslaved people to safeguard Island Ford Road. The finished fort had 15-foot-thick walls embedded with wooden palisades and abatis that protected the garrison from artillery fire and infantry assault. The work parties built other smaller redoubts and stockades to protect vital installations and connected

the whole with communications trenches. During the winter of 1780–1781, Cruger’s soldiers stockpiled provisions confiscated from local Whigs while butchers laid up barrels of salted beef and pork for the expected siege. Greene surveyed the enemy works with his chief engineer Colonel Kosciuszko on 22 May 1781. The reconnaissance revealed surprisingly strong defenses. Greene ordered his troops to bivouac out of cannon range and create hasty earthworks to cover the approaches to the town. Greene followed Kosciuszko’s advice to begin sapping operations toward the star fort, as they believed it to be the key to the enemy’s entire works. Ironically, the besiegers found themselves besieged, as later described by Greene: “The Tories swarm around us and render it extremely difficult to get either forage or subsistence for our Troops. We contend with the Enemy upon such an unequal footing that I have nothing less to expect than disgrace and ruin.” Greene’s troops found the encircled loyalists were equally daring and desperate. Kosciuszko placed the first battery position close enough to the enemy works to invite a surprise raid on 23 May 1781. The loyalist raiders killed and dispersed the American working party, seized their pioneer tools and several Black laborers, and withdrew into the star fort before Greene’s officers could respond.Chastened by the failure, the Americans collected more tools and built a second set of battery positions at a safe distance from the enemy. Under the cover of field guns and riflemen in the battery, fatigue parties of White soldiers and Black laborers dug zigzag approach trenches through the hard soil. At the same time, other American troops built a 40-foot-high Maham tower to sharpshoot the defenders. Cruger’s Tories responded by digging deeper and using the spoil to stack sandbags atop the redoubt walls. The monotony of the siege was broken when Lee and Pickens—with loyalist prisoners taken at Augusta—marched openly past the enemy redoubt into Greene’s camp on 8 June. The sight angered the loyalists inside Ninety Six and furthered their resolve to continue resistance. Greene used the fresh manpower to guard the garrison’s spring-fed water source. By 11 June, the loyalists were suffering from intense thirst in the

springtime heat, as they could only get water under the cover of darkness.On the same day, a messenger from Sumter arrived with news that Rawdon was en route with a relief force of 2,000 fresh British troops. Greene responded by asking Sumter and Marion to block the route, but a surprisingly stiff Tory militia response hindered them. Meanwhile, a loyalist courier bluffed his way past some inattentive Continental soldiers, which gave Cruger the first information about Rawdon’s relief expedition. Greene therefore had several unattractive options: remain in place and risk becoming trapped between Rawdon and Cruger; withdraw and admit that the siege had failed; or try to take Ninety Six by frontal assault. On 18 June 1781, Greene sent a Continental storming party against the star fort while the light infantry simultaneously attacked the redoubt guarding the spring. The assault troops breached the abatis and pulled down the sandbag parapet of the star fort as the sharpshooters in the Maham tower pinned down most of the defenders. However, Cruger’s disciplined provincials launched a surprise counterattack that overwhelmed the Continental breaching team, killing several American officers and dozens of their troops with bayonets and clubbed muskets. Greene’s forlorn hope had failed with the loss of 147 soldiers against 85 dead and injured Tories. Greene responded by lifting the siege and withdrawing before Rawdon could reach Ninety Six. Rawdon arrived on 21 June after a forced march through the torrid summertime heat, “Plan of the Siege of Ninety-Six,” in Benson J. Lossing, The Pictorial Field-book of the Revolution, vol. 2  (New York: Harper & Brothers, 1860)

which killed about fifty of the unacclimated new troops. Rawdon replaced his sickest troops with fit soldiers from Cruger’s garrison and attempted to pursue Greene. However, Lee and Washington’s dragoons screened the safe withdrawal of the main Continental force eastward across the Broad River. Greene thereby fulfilled his strategic objective of preserving his Continental force, but the withdrawal demoralized his troops and caused many Whig militiamen to desert to protect their property from loyalist retribution.Both sides tacitly suspended major operations to rest and prepare for the cooler fall season. Greene marched his army to the pro-patriot High Hills of the Santee, a quiet place to restore the health and morale of his army while he attended to strategic and administrative matters. Back in May 1781, Greene and Cornwallis had worked out a cartel for exchanging Continental and militia soldiers on a one-to-one basis, and exchange or parole for officers. The first American prisoners—including Benjamin Lincoln and William Moultrie—sailed in June from Charleston to Jamestown, Virginia. The ship then sailed to New York with a load of paroled British prisoners. The exchange was a welcome reprieve for the surviving Continental troops who had been held in Charleston; of the 2,700 taken prisoner in May 1780, only 1,300 were alive and available for exchange a year later. Greene suspended the agreement in August after the British executed Col. Isaac Hayne, a South Carolina militia officer, for breaking his parole. After an angry exchange of letters between Greene and Cornwallis, the prisoner exchanges resumed in October but only included officers. Besides worrying about the prisoner cartel, Greene wrote extensively to Steuben and Lafayette with guidance about defending Virginia from British raids.In the meantime, the British troops at Ninety Six loaded available wagons with casualties, provisions, and ordnance stores, while Rawdon told loyalist commanders to either abandon their land and move their households to Charleston or remain in place without British protection. About 800 loyalists and their families marched southward with Rawdon’s corps. The Tories who remained in the Ninety Six district soon regretted their decision, as many were hanged and their houses burned despite Greene’s orders forbidding

such practices. Greene described the brutal nature of the civil war within South Carolina to Col. Alexander Hamilton: “The division among the people is much greater than I imagined, and the Whigs and Tories persecute each other, with little less than savage fury. There is nothing but murders and devastations in every quarter.” A lull in the campaign followed the British departure as both sides rested their regular troops. Operations did not cease during the summer. Lee’s and Marion’s light troops continued to attack British outposts on the Santee River—the last easily defendable terrain feature north of Charleston—while Pickens’s militia skirmished with loyalist and Cherokee raiders led by Major William “Bloody Bill” Cunningham.

Greene returned to active operations in early September 1781 with a well-drilled force of roughly 2,500 soldiers: 1,250 Continentals, 300 dragoons, and 150 South Carolina state troops, plus some 700 militiamen commanded by Marion and Pickens. The morale of the army had recovered, and most of the Continentals and militiamen were battle-tested and confident. Greene, however, was dogged continually by supply shortages, especially uniforms and equipment. By contrast, Lt. Col. Alexander Stewart commanded an army of 1,400 soldiers: Maj. John Marjoribanks’s light infantry battalion, three regiments of British regulars, Cruger’s provincial battalion, a small dragoon squadron, and five guns. Stewart had no shortage of equipment and ordnance stores, but at this point, the British had great difficulty obtaining fresh provisions and forage in the face of persistent rebel militia attacks. Stewart’s regulars were mostly fresh recruits unused to southern diseases and heat and untested in battle. Each army had a sizeable number of both deserters and former prisoners of war who enlisted (willingly or not) to fight against their former comrades. At this stage in the war, both the British and American armies routinely hanged any recaptured deserters, thus motivating some to fight hard to avoid capture.

Each side also operated under a new strategic paradigm. Back in June 1781, Greene learned from congressional president Samuel Huntington that Russia had offered to broker a peace treaty based on the Roman concept of uti possidetis, which granted each belligerent a right to the territory it controlled or occupied at the cessation of the conflict. King George III was receptive to the idea, as he could extract Britain from an increasingly costly war while retaining Georgia and South Carolina as lucrative consolation prizes. Greene responded by adjusting his strategy to establish Whig military and political hegemony over the region, which he described in a letter to Georgia justice John Wilkinson: Upon a consultation I can think of no better mode for the State to  .  .  . secure itself from the further ravages of the enemy than to form a Council . . . whose orders should have the force of Laws. . . . You may rely upon my giving you all the protection in my power; but the people must take measures not only for their own internal security but to aid the Continental Army. . . . Two evils which prevail in all the Southern States should be checked.  .  .  plundering and private murders.  .  .  . Appointing a Councel, raising a body of regular State troops, forming, arming and arranging the Militia . . . and destroying the enemy fortifications should be the first object of peoples attention.Greene understood that political sovereignty rested on the acquiescence, if not consent, of the civilians to Whig governance. Greene thus redoubled his efforts to tamp down on the Whig-on-Tory abuses and promote fair treatment of civilians by the Continentals and militia alike. Greene then pressured South Carolina Governor John Rutledge and surviving members of the state’s privy council to reestablish governance in South Carolina. Georgia had no existing Whig government, so Greene dispatched Deputy Paymaster Joseph Clay, a former member of Georgia’s provincial congress, to lay the groundwork for a pro-American government.

Greene’s efforts along political and economic lines were for naught unless he drove the British and loyalist troops from the remaining interior bases. Greene pressured southern partisan commanders to redouble their attacks on British outposts and patrols. (See Map 7.) Marion and Pickens remained cooperative, and Sumter offered to cooperate but soon thereafter unilaterally discharged his troops after a botched attack at Biggin Church in late August. Greene nevertheless set out to stop Stewart’s reprovisioning patrols above the Santee River. Greene’s intelligence showed Stewart had a sizeable force camped at Thompson’s Plantation, near the strategically important McCord’s Ferry on the Santee River. Although the straight-line distance from the High Hills to McCord’s Ferry was approximately 40 miles, Greene led his army northward to cross the Wateree River at Camden—a detour that added 30 miles while bypassing the obvious approach march across the rain-swollen terrain between the Congaree and Santee Rivers. Greene’s ruse did not fool Stewart, and he responded by relocating his corps to Eutaw Springs—a location where a sturdy two-story brick house formed a convenient strong point overlooking the Charleston road. Eutaw Springs also afforded access to spring water, forage, provisions, and reinforcements from Charleston. Greene left his logistics trains at Motte’s Fort after learning of Stewart’s location at Eutaw Springs. Greene’s combat troops bivouacked at Burdell’s Plantation, only 7 miles west of Eutaw Springs, on the evening of 7 September 1781.The American army began its movement at 0400 on 8 September 1781, with Lee’s reinforced legion as the advanced guard. Shortly thereafter, Stewart dispatched a foraging detachment of 300 soldiers drawn from every regiment. By happenstance, the “rooting party” avoided detection by marching to a plantation well off the River Road. Stewart first learned of Greene’s advance from two North Carolina deserters, and he responded with a combat patrol of 140 infantry and 50 dragoons under Maj. John Coffin. Coffin’s dragoons began the battle by killing two American dragoons during an engagement around 0800 hours. Lee responded by luring Coffin’s squadron into an ambush, where fire from the American light infantrymen unhorsed Coffin and struck down ten loyalist dragoons and half the

light infantrymen in a bloody firefight. The fighting drew the lightly armed foraging party into the open, where Lee’s light infantry quickly overran them. Many unwounded British troops avoided capture by dropping their weapons and running into the woods. At a stroke, Greene’s army had eliminated about a regiment’s worth of troops from Stewart’s order of battle—even before the start of the main engagement.Stewart reacted to the sounds of firing by sending out a covering force to screen the deployment of the remaining infantry into a line of battle west of the brick house. Major Marjoribanks’s light troops took position on the right flank by sheltering in a thicket of blackjack oak alongside Eutaw Creek. The remnants of Coffin’s light troops and the field guns took up a blocking position on the road to Charleston. Stewart positioned the available soldiers of the 3d Foot, 84th Highlanders, Cruger’s Loyalists, and the 64th and 63d Foot into a line of battle. Stewart commanded about 2,000 regulars and provincials after accounting for last-minute reinforcements and his earlier losses. By 0900, Greene had his army arrayed in a three-line attack formation, with the North and South Carolina militia in the first line. The Continentals were next, with the Maryland regiments on the left, Virginians in the middle, and the new North Carolina Continentals on the right. Greene next positioned Washington’s 2d Partisan Corps and Kirkwood’s Delaware light infantry in reserve and anchored his flanks with dragoons under Col. Wade Hampton and Colonel Lee. Greene lastly positioned a 3-pounder section in the militia line, and 6-pounder guns with the Continentals. Greene commanded a force of 2,076 officers and troops, of which 856 were Continentals. The remainder were state line and militia troops. Despite the season and time of day, the weather was described as hot and sultry, enough to cause heat exhaustion and heat stroke among the ranks during the battle.The patriot militia showed themselves the equals of their British and Tory opponents in the opening minutes of the battle. Unlike earlier battles, the militiamen advanced into firing range and stayed there for several minutes, trading volleys with the enemy. Discipline in the Whig ranks was so good that subordinates replaced wounded

commanders without the unit becoming noticeably disordered. After perhaps fifteen minutes of close combat, Greene ordered the exhausted militia line to break contact and regroup behind General Jethro Sumner’s North Carolina Continentals. The North Carolinians fought stubbornly against Stewart’s main line, which prompted the commanders of the 63d and 64th Foot to respond with a bayonet charge. The British troops drove back the North Carolinians but were in turn disordered by a riposte from Lee’s light troops. Greene countered by committing the Virginia and Maryland Continentals. At this point, Stewart’s troops in the center and left had fought two engagements already, so the onrush of four fresh Continental regiments was too much for the fatigued redcoats to handle. The 64th Foot was hit in front and flank and broke in panic, compelling the remainder to fall back to regroup at the brick house. The disorder affected the Americans as well, as they had to contend with disarming prisoners and fending off enemy dragoons while trying to pursue the broken enemy. Losses were heavy in the American ranks, with several commanders killed or wounded. Greene seemingly had victory in his grasp, and he committed Washington’s dragoons and Kirkwood’s light infantry to exploit the disorder and crush the demoralized redcoats.Yet success again eluded Greene, this time because of Major Marjoribanks’s light infantry. Their stubborn defense in the blackjack thicket on the British right allowed Maj. Henry Sheridan and a company of New York Volunteers time to barricade themselves in the brick house. Washington unaccountably erred by not waiting for his light infantry support before leading his dragoons to attack Marjoribanks’s position. Marjoribanks’s troops quickly shot down about half the American troopers, including Washington, who was bayoneted and captured while pinned underneath his wounded horse. Hampton regrouped the unwounded troopers and drove Marjoribanks’s light infantry from the thicket with support from Kirkwood’s light infantry. Greene described the climax of the battle to Continental Congress President Thomas McKean:

We kept close at the Enemy’s heels after they broke . . . and a great number of Prisoners were continually falling into our hands, and some hundreds of the Fugitives ran off. . . . But a party threw themselves into a large three story brick House  .  .  . others were lodged in an impenetrable thicket.  .  .  . Thus secured in front, and upon the right by the House, and a deep Ravine upon the left. . . . Every exertion was made to dislodge them. Lt. Col. Washington made the most astonishing efforts . . . to charge the Enemy in the Rear but found it impracticable, had his Horse shot under him, and was wounded and taken Prisoner. Four six pounders were ordered up before the house . . . and they were pushed on so much under the command of the fire from the House . . . and Thickett as rendered it impracticable to bring them off again when the Troops were ordered to retire. . . . Nothing but the brick House, and the peculiar strength of the position at Battle of Eutaw Springs, Alonzo Chappel, 1858  (New York Public Library)

Eutaw saved the remains of the British army from being all made Prisoners. Greene’s report glossed over how his army fell into disorder after breaking the enemy line and pursuing the disorganized remnants through the British bivouac site—where some accounts describe the American troops pausing to plunder enemy rum and provisions. Heavy losses among Greene’s officers exacerbated the breakdown in command and control. Both Lt. Col. John Eager Howard of the 1st Maryland and Lt. Col. William Washington received bayonet wounds that took them out of combat, and Col. Richard Campbell, the commander of the Virginia brigade, was killed in action. Meanwhile, Major Sheridan’s Volunteers in the brick house checked the American advance with heavy fire and a quick counterattack that seized two cannons and several Continental prisoners. Greene conceded defeat after two hours of punishing combat and ordered his troops to break contact and withdraw, bringing with them the wounded who were not within range of the British guns. The remaining British troops tried to pursue aggressively but were halted by Hampton’s dragoon rear guard. Greene withdrew his battered army back to its campsite at Burdell’s Plantation while Stewart regrouped his troops near the brick house. Stewart and Greene then worked out the disposition of prisoners and wounded through an exchange of letters. Continental surgeons sent the sick and wounded to the army hospital at Camden, while militiamen escorted the British and loyalist prisoners northward to Salisbury, North Carolina. In the meantime, the British troops buried their dead and loaded up the wounded and movable supplies. The redcoats then destroyed excess muskets, rum, and provisions before withdrawing on 10 September. Greene ordered Lee and Marion to harass the enemy’s withdrawal, but rain and reinforcements from Charleston helped screen Stewart’s withdrawal to the upper Cooper River near Monck’s Corner. Both sides lost heavily in the Eutaw Springs engagement. A postbattle tally of Greene’s forces showed 139 killed, 375 wounded, and 8 missing in action—about 25 percent of Greene’s combat strength. By contrast,

Stewart reported losses of 84 dead, 351 wounded, and 257 missing in action—roughly 13 percent of his corps. Greene claimed to have taken 500 prisoners, thus leaving Stewart with about 1,100 soldiers still fit for duty.Both sides claimed victory. Greene based his claim on the haul of prisoners and weapons, whereas Stewart pointed to his possession of the battlefield and several Continental cannons as prizes. Stewart won in a narrow tactical sense because of the tenaciousness of Marjoribanks’s defense of the ravine and Sheridan’s stand at the brick house. Yet, much as at Guilford Courthouse and Hobkirk Hill, Stewart’s tactical victory was strategically barren. General Leslie, the overall British commander, was compelled to contract his defensive perimeter to Dorchester, on the upper Ashley River, and Goose Creek, a tributary of the Cooper River. Despite the British withdrawal, die-hard loyalist bands along the border of South and North Carolina continued to fight against local patriot patrols.

The euphoria in the American ranks from the Eutaw Springs battle soon evaporated, and Greene had his hands full dealing with a sick, hungry, and discontented army. Greene responded by using patriot patrols to watch the British while he marched his Continentals back to their habitual campsite along the Santee River. Meanwhile, Greene did what he could to shape operations in Virginia and North Carolina and worked on prisoner exchanges with Leslie. At the same time, his officers nursed the army back to health and prepared to resume the campaign in cooler weather. Greene received welcome news in late October when he learned of General Cornwallis’s surrender at Yorktown. Soon thereafter, Greene received an offer from Leslie to resume prisoner exchanges—an offer Greene spurned over his resentment of Isaac Hayne’s execution. Greene also learned that the Continental Congress had voted their thanks to the individual units and particular officers for the Eutaw Springs battle. Congress especially honored Greene with the award of a gold medal commemorating what they saw as a victory at Eutaw Springs.

Cornwallis’s surrender did nothing to change matters in North America immediately (Map 8). Clinton still commanded 15,000 combat troops in New York alone, and the British army and Royal Navy had substantial combat forces in the West Indies. Within the southern theater, the British still controlled roughly 9,000 British regulars and provincials, and hundreds more loyalist supporters. Hardcore loyalists continued to launch raids from Charleston and Savannah, and in several instances, they inflicted heavy losses on isolated rebel patrols. However, the surrender at Yorktown demoralized the British troops so much that their commanders refused to continue risking troops in unnecessary offensive operations. Greene led a reconnaissance force toward Dorchester in November 1781, which encountered only scattered resistance from loyalist partisans, while General Leslie quietly withdrew the Dorchester garrison down to Charleston.

Despite the high operational tempo during the summer of 1781, Greene never lost sight of his strategic goal of ending the Whig-vs.-Tory civil war and establishing undisputed American sovereignty in the region. For example, Greene repeatedly urged Whig militia leaders to rein in the counterproductive habit of brutalizing Tory prisoners, news of which discouraged many loyalists from deserting. In addition, Greene convinced Governor Rutledge to pardon loyalists who successfully served a tour in patriot militia ranks. Rutledge further encouraged loyalist defections through a confiscation act that legalized the seizure of property from staunch Tories. The combination of carrot and stick induced many loyalists to quietly leave Charleston and submit to patriot authority.Greene prioritized his efforts on Georgia, which he judged would be the easiest to control. Greene prodded the congressional delegates from Georgia to take the lead: The enemy Have but little footing in that State [Georgia] and if proper regulations could take place it would

be difficult for them ever to gain ground there again without a very great force. . . . I have recommended to the people to choose a council to govern their affairs until a Legislature could be at hand; and I wish from the . . . European intelligence  .  .  . that a compleat Legislature agreeable to the constitution could be formed as soon as possible.Greene assisted the Georgians by ordering Deputy Paymaster Clay to redouble his efforts to smooth out factional disputes among the Georgia Whigs and prepare for elections. Greene backed the Georgia Map 8

politicians with force by mustering Col. Elijah Clarke’s state militia troops into Continental service, thereby bolstering American claims of control over the state. Greene’s efforts to consolidate American sovereignty in Georgia culminated in August 1781 with the election of Nathan Brownson, a physician who had represented Georgia at the Second Continental Congress, as governor by the state legislature. However, the departure of many of the Maryland troops and officers at the end of their term of service in late 1782 complicated Greene’s operational plans. Greene had anticipated the impending loss and demanded reinforcements from the fresh Continental troops released by the British surrender at Yorktown. Greene also wrote directly to Marshal Jean-Baptiste-Donatien de Vimeur, comte de Rochambeau, commander of the French blockading fleet at Yorktown, asking for a similar operation against Charleston. General Washington’s focus was on Clinton’s army in New York, so he promised Greene only a single Continental brigade of Pennsylvanians under Brig. Gen. Anthony Wayne. Although Wayne did not arrive until December, his march southward prompted the British evacuation of Wilmington—thus ending a permanent British presence in North Carolina.In the interim, Greene did what he could to tighten the screws on the British enclave at Charleston. Greene moved his headquarters to the village of Round O, which lay astride the British lines of communications between Savannah and Charleston. Greene then positioned his available manpower in a loose cordon around Charleston: Continentals along the Edisto River to the west and south, and light forces east of the Cooper River at Monck’s Corner. Leslie exploited Greene’s weakness with periodic raids by loyalist forces, which included a troop of Black dragoons that Leslie shrewdly had recruited from among the formerly enslaved Black volunteers in December 1781. The Black dragoons proved formidable opponents, as they had intimate knowledge of the terrain and rebel sympathizers—and would fight hard to avoid capture and reenslavement. In February 1782, one such raiding detachment battered Marion’s militiamen so badly that they withdrew back to the Santee River. Meanwhile, Greene

tried other schemes to keep the British off balance, such as a raid in January 1782 that failed to capture the 500-odd British defenders of Johns Island. Greene also failed to convince Georgia and South Carolina to adopt a proposal by Lt. Col. John Laurens—son of the former president of the Continental Congress, Henry Laurens—to enlist enslaved Black volunteers and promise them their freedom after the war. Greene found that most civil officials believed the end of the war was in sight and balked at the additional cost of providing fresh recruits and supplies to sustain his force. Greene relieved some of the camp chores from his combat troops by using about 500 enslaved Black noncombatants for wagoner and engineer work. Wayne’s fresh Continentals joined the Southern army in January 1782, giving Greene the combat power necessary to consolidate American gains in the region. Georgia was uppermost in Greene’s mind, as British and loyalist forces still held territory west of the Savannah River. Greene’s strategic approach of subordinating the military to civil authority and governance was reflected in his orders to General Wayne:You will therefore march  .  .  . the whole of your force . . . for covering the Country. . . . You will open an immediate correspondence with the Governor . . . make such requisitions for militia, as you may find requisite. . . . The mode of subsisting your troops will also concert with the magistrates of the state . . . be as little oppressive as possible to the people. When you get into the lower Country you will invite all people to join . . . afford them protection & security. Try by every means in your power to soften the  .  .  . deadly resentments subsisting between the Whigs and tories, and put a stop as much as possible to that cruel custom of putting people to death after they have surrendered. . . . The practice of plundering you will endeavor to Check as much as possible. . . . Let your discipline be as regular

and as rigid, as the nature and constitution of your troops will admit.With matters in Georgia moving to a climax, Greene moved to finish the job in South Carolina. The state convened its first elected General Assembly and elected John Mathews as the new governor in January 1782. The new state government was installed at Jacksonboro, a town only 30 miles from Charleston, thereby threatening British claims to control the territory. Although Greene was unaware at the time, the end of the war was near at hand. French seizures of British holdings in the Caribbean and Mediterranean magnified the psychological impact of Cornwallis’s surrender in October 1781. The British government collapsed in February 1782 after the House of Commons refused to support the king’s plans to retain footholds in Georgia and South Carolina. The new opposition party quickly concluded that the American holdings were too small and isolated to defend easily from further French and Spanish attacks. Consequently, the new British prime minister, Charles Watson-Wentworth, 2nd Marquess of Rockingham, began measures to wind down the war in North America. Rockingham replaced General Clinton with Lt. Gen. Sir Guy Carleton, who had a mandate to evacuate troops safely from New York, Charleston, and Savannah—and to use that manpower to beef up the defense of the West Indies. Rockingham reorganized the political structure in North America under the sole authority of Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs Charles Fox. Rockingham then directed Secretary of State for Home and Colonial Affairs William Petty, 2nd Earl of Shelburne, to open peace negotiations. After months of diplomatic wrangling, British, French, and American representatives signed preliminary peace agreements on 20 January 1783. The War of American Independence ended officially in Paris on 3 September 1783. The Americans won their full independence and important fishing and Appalachian territorial concessions in exchange for dropping claims

to Canada and Florida. British territorial losses were limited largely to the American colonies, and the British retained Gibraltar and their most valuable colonies in the West Indies. Most importantly, Britain had extricated itself from a costly and unpopular war without permanently severing diplomatic and economic ties with the Americans.In anticipation of the upcoming peace treaty, Carleton ordered Leslie in June 1782 to prepare for an orderly withdrawal from Charleston, Savannah, and East Florida once sufficient transport was available. Leslie sat on the orders until 7 August as he feared the adverse effect on the morale of his loyalist supporters. Leslie’s fears were realized when panic ensued in Charleston after the orders were published. Greene soon learned of the order from a steady stream of demoralized loyalists leaving Charleston. Greene responded by ordering his pickets to turn back the Tory defectors to add pressure on Leslie—an order largely ignored by his troops, who had compassion on the loyalist refugees. Governor Mathews responded by offering amnesty to lukewarm Tories and proper judicial proceedings for the most notorious loyalist leaders. Mathews’s proclamation was accepted by many Tory insurgents who were demoralized by the imminent British evacuation and patriot and friendly Creek patrols eventually eliminated the remaining loyalist holdouts. In Charleston, Leslie sought to end an increasingly pointless conflict by halting shipment of weapons and ammunition to loyalist and emancipated partisans, and seeking a truce—an overture rejected by a suspicious Greene.In the meantime, Greene felt he had to keep pressure on the British to convince them to end the war, not just redeploy their combat forces to resume operations in New York. Yet the lack of reinforcements, funds, and supplies from Philadelphia and the states in his department continually hamstrung Greene’s efforts. Greene was so desperate for supplies that he quietly authorized the exchange of provisions for clothing from loyalist manufacturers in Charleston. Greene was also faced with keeping his increasingly sick and disaffected army together through a long and frustrating summer of containing the British in their coastal enclaves. At one point, tempers

boiled over when disaffected soldiers in Wayne’s Pennsylvania Line articulated plans for mutiny in protest against shortfalls in pay and provisions. The Pennsylvanians, several of whom were British deserters, had mutinied once before at Morristown in late 1780. Greene moved swiftly to squelch the mutiny by publicly executing the ringleader after a swift court-martial. The remaining mutineers received dishonorable discharges, and as part of their punishment they and their families were sent to work rolling cartridges at the logistics depot at Salisbury, North Carolina. British control of Georgia, meanwhile, ebbed under pressure from Clarke’s militia and Wayne’s Continentals. Governor John Martin replaced Governor Brownson in early 1782 and offered pardons to loyalists who enlisted in state line or militia service, an enticement that convinced many lukewarm Tories to defect. Meanwhile, Royal Governor Sir James Wright and the remaining die-hard loyalists fought a losing battle to retain a foothold in the state’s interior. Wright’s frustration at the lack of reinforcements culminated with receiving a humiliating order to evacuate Georgia—days after celebrating the king’s birthday in Savannah on 4 June 1782. After a final round of skirmishes between loyalist rangers and Creek auxiliaries with Lt. Col. James Jackson’s Georgia Legion, Governor Wright oversaw the evacuation of Savannah on 11 July 1782. The evacuation transplanted 2,000 White loyalists and about 4,000 freed Black loyalists to St. Augustine, with a further 400 White settlers and 5,000 enslaved Black people sailing to Jamaica. Those who settled in Florida were later repatriated when Britain ceded the territory to Spain in the final peace treaty of 1783. The triumphant Georgia Whigs convened the new General Assembly in January 1783 and elected Lyman Hall as the next governor. However, the Georgia state troops and militia remained busy for several months, mopping up isolated detachments of Tories and pro-British Creek and Cherokee tribal combatants.Both sides knew the end was in sight in South Carolina, but occasional skirmishes still happened between foraging patrols. One such firefight on the Combahee River on 27 August 1782 resulted in the death of Colonel Laurens, a loss that Greene decried as a

needless, “paltry little skirmish.” In the meantime, Leslie began the evacuation of loyalist and American provincial troops—followed by prominent loyalists and their families, enslaved laborers, and personal property—from Charleston to St. Augustine and Nova Scotia in October 1782. The last engagement in the South probably occurred on 14 November 1782, when a Continental patrol clashed with an armed woodcutting party on James Island. By 13 December 1782, the British had assembled 130 transports and escorts at Charleston to carry the remaining 4,000 British regulars and provincials, loyalists, and about 5,300 free and enslaved Black people. In the interim, Greene had positioned detachments closer to the city, hoping for an opportunity to attack. Intelligence soon indicated an evacuation was imminent for 12 December, so Greene ordered Wayne to take a strong reconnaissance force—300 light infantry, 80 dragoons, and an artillery detachment—across to the Neck to harass the British. Wayne halted the movement when a courier under a flag of truce presented Greene a proposal from General Leslie, which promised a peaceful evacuation of Charleston if Greene’s troops would hold their fire until complete. Greene gratefully accepted Leslie’s terms and promptly canceled Wayne’s reconnaissance in force. Early on 14 December 1782, Greene and General William Moultrie—the victor of Sullivan’s Island in 1776 and a former British prisoner of war—crossed the Ashley to oversee the final act. The British fired a cannon from the Hornwork, the citadel guarding the city’s entrance, to signal the beginning of their withdrawal. Both sides warily watched one another for any sign of hostilities until the British rear guard passed through the city gates at the vacant Hornwork. While the British troops marched eastward to their transports on the Cooper River. Wayne’s troops continued southward to secure the South Carolina State House. Greene’s security detachment then escorted newly elected Governor Mathews and the Privy Council to occupy the House, all in full view of the British fleet slowly making its way toward open waters. The governor officially marked the end of the British occupation on Sunday, 15 December 1782. As General Moultrie noted afterward: “It was an

ample reward for the triumphant soldier, after all the hazards and fatigues of war, which he had gone through, to be the instrument of releasing his friends and fellow citizens from captivity, and restoring to them their liberties and possessions of their city and country again.”Between 1775 and 1783, the British army suffered perhaps 6,800 combat deaths. By contrast, more than 25,000 Americans died from all causes during the war. Available data indicate that about 852 Americans were killed and 1,198 wounded in action—about 10  percent of the total casualties—during the southern campaign of 1781–1783. Continental officers and militiamen who died in or shortly after combat generally received proper burials, but the dead Continental troops, mostly soldiers from Maryland and Delaware, were buried where they fell. Their remains thus render each southern battlefield hallowed ground to the cause of American freedom.Congress officially disbanded the Southern Army on 25 November 1783. Enlisted troops with an established trade or family homestead usually went home to rebuild their lives. Those who lacked prewar ties moved westward to take advantage of their freedoms, and later, land bounties and pensions. Nathanael Greene’s business fortunes suffered during the war, compounding the debts he incurred to buy supplies for the Southern Army. He received no debt relief from a cash-strapped Congress but was helped by land grants from grateful Georgia and North Carolina citizens. Greene settled on a plantation near Savannah, but he died of a stroke on 19 June 1786 before he could turn a profit. Daniel Morgan briefly returned to service to defend Virginia in mid-1781, but chronic sciatica and rheumatism forced his retirement near Winchester, Virginia. There, he married and dabbled in politics and land speculation before dying peacefully in 1802. Many other former Continental officers moved naturally into civil governance roles. Otho Holland Williams served as commissioner of the Port of Baltimore and later as a United States Representative before his death in 1794. John Eager Howard briefly resumed his profitable enterprises in Baltimore, Maryland, before

serving as the state’s governor and representing the state in both houses of the U.S. Congress. Henry Lee played a prominent role in the last Congress of the Confederation and the 1787 Constitutional Convention. He subsequently was elected governor of Virginia from 1791 to 1794 and served one term in Congress. Lee later fell into debt and ill health before dying in 1818. South Carolinians lionized William Moultrie and elected him to the state legislature. He served two terms as governor before his death at Charleston in 1805. Andrew Pickens resumed planting and served as a tribal negotiator and member of the U.S. House of Representatives before passing away in 1817. A penniless Thomas Sumter represented South Carolina at the 1787 Constitutional Convention and served three terms in the U.S. House and Senate before his death in 1832. Francis Marion served briefly in politics before returning home to marry his cousin, Mary Esther Videau. He also served as commander of Fort Johnson, outside Charleston. Cornwallis returned home after surrendering at Yorktown, where his humiliation was assuaged by honors from King George III. Clinton was widely blamed for the loss of America. He retained his commission but was relegated to minor posts while he served in Parliament. Francis Rawdon returned home to recover from malaria and received honors and promotions, dying in 1826 as the 1st Marquess of Hastings.Over time, Continentals and militiamen were compensated for lost wages through land grants and pensions and were honored in the postwar historical narratives. Camp followers played an essential part in sustaining the war effort yet received no similar recognition for their service. Native tribes in the southern states fared poorly regardless of which side they supported. The Catawba nation sided with the Americans and suffered heavily during the fighting of 1780–1781, which left the postwar Catawba tribe a shrunken, impoverished remnant in the Carolinas. By contrast, the Cherokee lost dozens of their settlements during fighting in 1776, with the surviving bands driven westward across the mountains. The British outraged their former allies by ceding the trans-Appalachia territory to the Americans, thus setting the stage for future American-Cherokee conflict. Many wealthy southern loyalists went into exile, some going

to Jamaica, and smaller numbers settling in Nova Scotia or Britain. In later years, many exiles received compensation in the form of land grants or pensions. A small number of loyalists, generally those not suspected of violent crimes, remained in the South. The climate of reconciliation fostered by Greene and Rutledge—assisted by prewar business and family connections—allowed many loyalists to integrate into postwar society quietly. The fate of the enslaved Black population varied widely. Many exiled slave-holding loyalists opened new plantations in the West Indies. The British, however, honored offers of emancipation to the surviving Black dragoons and other Black soldiers who joined the war effort before 30 November 1782. Many freed Black people emigrated to Nova Scotia, where they experienced harsh living conditions and discrimination over jobs and land grants. Their lot was still better than the many thousands of enslaved people who remained behind in the southern states. They would remain in bondage until the final destruction of slavery during the American Civil War of 1861–1865. Although often overlooked in American histories of the War of Independence, the French lost several thousand dead and sick and incurred (in today’s dollars) about half a trillion dollars in costs—which included millions of dollars in direct loans and the furnishing of military-grade supplies and weapons to equip Continental regiments. Spain also played an indirect role, though it never entered a formal alliance out of fear that the rebellion would spread to its own American colonies. The actions of Spain’s navy as a check against the British freed up the French navy to support Washington’s forces at Yorktown, and Spanish expeditions against Pensacola and Mobile further strained British resources. Lastly, Spanish pesos and credit, and essential supplies like gunpowder and cinchona bark, helped to sustain the American war effort in the South.
